senses.d: An exclamation denoting surprise, joy, or grief. Both as uttered and as written, it expresses a great variety of emotions, determined by the tone or the context. When repeated, ha, ha, it is an expression of laughter, satisfaction, or triumph, sometimes of derisive laughter; or sometimes it is equivalent to “Well, it is so.”
q: Ha-has, and inarticulate hootings of satirical rebuke.

senses.d: Properly, a short hauberk, but often used loosely for the hauberk.

Habergeon.etym: [F. haubergeon a small hauberk, dim. of OF. hauberc, F. haubert. See Hauberk.]

senses.d: Capable of being inhabited; that may be inhabited or dwelt in; as, the habitable world.
The act of inhabiting; state of inhabiting or dwelling, or of being inhabited; occupancy.
Place of abode; settled dwelling; residence; house.
q: The Lord . . . blesseth the habitation of the just.

senses.d: A handle; that part of an instrument or vessel taken into the hand, and by which it is held and used; — said chiefly of a knife, sword, or dagger; the hilt.
q: This brandish'd dagger I'll bury to the haft in her fair breast.

senses.d: A dwelling.

Haft.etym: [AS. hæft; akin to D. & G. heft, Icel. hepti, and to E. heave, or have. Cf. Heft.]

senses.d: To set in, or furnish with, a haft; as, to haft a dagger.
Small roundish masses of ice precipitated from the clouds, where they are formed by the congelation of vapor. The separate masses or grains are called hailstones.
q: Thunder mixed with hail, Hail mixed with fire, must rend the Egyptian sky.

Hail.etym: [OE. hail, ha”el, AS. hægel, hagol; akin to D., G., Dan., & Sw. hagel; Icel. hagl; cf. Gr. κάχληξ pebble.]

senses.d: To pour down particles of ice, or frozen vapors.
To pour forcibly down, as hail.
Healthy. See Hale (the preferable spelling).
To call loudly to, or after; to accost; to salute; to address.
To name; to designate; to call.
q: And such a son as all men hailed me happy.

Hail.etym: [OE. hailen, heilen, Icel. heill hale, sound, used in greeting. See Hale sound.]

senses.d: To declare, by hailing, the port from which a vessel sails or where she is registered; hence, to sail; to come; — used with from; as, the steamer hails from New York.
To report as one's home or the place from whence one comes; to come; — with from.
An exclamation of respectful or reverent salutation, or, occasionally, of familiar greeting.
A wish of health; a salutation; a loud call.
q: The angel hail bestowed.

senses.d: A single particle of ice falling from a cloud; a frozen raindrop; a pellet of hail.
The collection or mass of filaments growing from the skin of an animal, and forming a covering for a part of the head or for any part or the whole of the body.
One the above-mentioned filaments, consisting, in vertebrate animals, of a long, tubular part which is free and flexible, and a bulbous root imbedded in the skin.
q: Then read he me how Sampson lost his hairs.
And draweth new delights with hoary hairs.

senses.d: Hair (human or animal) used for various purposes; as, hair for stuffing cushions.

A slender outgrowth from the chitinous cuticle of insects, spiders, crustaceans, and other invertebrates. Such hairs are totally unlike those of vertebrates in structure, composition, and mode of growth.
An outgrowth of the epidermis, consisting of one or of several cells, whether pointed, hooked, knobbed, or stellated. Internal hairs occur in the flower stalk of the yellow frog lily (Nuphar).
A spring device used in a hair-trigger firearm.
A haircloth.
Any very small distance, or degree; a hairbreadth.

Hair.etym: [OE. her, heer, hær, AS. hǣr; akin to OFries. hēr, D. & G. haar, OHG. & Icel. hār, Dan. haar, Sw. hår; cf. Lith. kasa.]

senses.d: Bearing or covered with hair; made of or resembling hair; rough with hair; hirsute.
q: His mantle hairy, and his bonnet sedge.

senses.d: Sound; entire; healthy; robust; not impaired; as, a hale body.
q: Last year we thought him strong and hale.

Hale.etym: [OE. heil, Icel. heill; akin to E. whole. See Whole.]

senses.d: Welfare.
q: All heedless of his dearest hale.

senses.d: To pull; to drag; to haul.
q: Easier both to freight, and to hale ashore.
As some dark priest hales the reluctant victim.

Hale.etym: [OE. halen, halien; cf. AS. holian, to acquire, get. See Haul.]

senses.d: Consisting of a moiety, or half; as, a half bushel; a half hour; a half dollar; a half view.
Consisting of some indefinite portion resembling a half; approximately a half, whether more or less; partial; imperfect; as, a half dream; half knowledge.
q: Assumed from thence a half consent.

Half.etym: [AS. healf, half, half; as a noun, half, side, part; akin to OS., OFries., & D. half, G. halb, Sw. half, Dan. halv, Icel. hālfr, Goth. halbs. Cf. Halve, Behalf.]

senses.d: In an equal part or degree; in some part approximating a half; partially; imperfectly; as, half-colored, half done, half-hearted, half persuaded, half conscious.
q: Their children spoke halfin the speech of Ashdod.

senses.d: Part; side; behalf.
q: The four halves of the house.

senses.d: One of two equal parts into which anything may be divided, or considered as divided; — sometimes followed by of; as, a half of an apple.
q: Not half his riches known, and yet despised.
A friendship so complete Portioned in halves between us.

senses.d: To halve. See Halve.
A building or room of considerable size and stateliness, used for public purposes; as, Westminster Hall, in London.

The chief room in a castle or manor house, and in early times the only public room, serving as the place of gathering for the lord's family with the retainers and servants, also for cooking and eating. It was often contrasted with the bower, which was the private or sleeping apartment.
q: Full sooty was her bower and eke her hall.

senses.d: A vestibule, entrance room, etc., in the more elaborated buildings of later times.
Any corridor or passage in a building.
A name given to many manor houses because the magistrate's court was held in the hall of his mansion; a chief mansion house.
A college in an English university (at Oxford, an unendowed college).
The apartment in which English university students dine in common; hence, the dinner itself; as, hall is at six o'clock.
Cleared passageway in a crowd; — formerly an exclamation.

Hall.etym: [OE. halle, hal, AS. heal, heall; akin to D. hal, OS. & OHG. halla, G. halle, Icel. höll, and prob. from a root meaning, to hide, conceal, cover. See Hell, Helmet.]

senses.d: To make holy; to set apart for holy or religious use; to consecrate; to treat or keep as sacred; to reverence.
q: Hallow the Sabbath day, to do no work therein.
His secret altar touched with hallowed fire.
In a larger sense . . . we can not hallow this ground .

Hallow.etym: [OE. halowen, halwien, halgien, AS. hālgian, fr. hālig holy. See Holy.]

senses.d: A stop in marching or walking, or in any action; arrest of progress.
q: Without any halt they marched.
soon in passion's war contest, Yet in their march soon make a halt.

Halt.etym: [Formerly alt, It. alto, G. halt, fr. halten to hold. See Hold.]

senses.d: To hold one's self from proceeding; to hold up; to cease progress; to stop for a longer or shorter period; to come to a stop; to stand still.
To stand in doubt whether to proceed, or what to do; to hesitate; to be uncertain.
q: How long halt ye between two opinions?

senses.d: To cause to cease marching; to stop; as, the general halted his troops for refreshment.
Halting or stopping in walking; lame.
q: Bring in hither the poor, and the maimed, and the halt, and the blind.

Halt.etym: [AS. healt; akin to OS., Dan., & Sw. halt, Icel. haltr, halltr, Goth. halts, OHG. halz.]

senses.d: The act of limping; lameness.
To walk lamely; to limp.
To have an irregular rhythm; to be defective.
q: The blank verse shall halt for it.

Halt.etym: [OE. halten, AS. healtian. See Halt, a.]

senses.d: Home.
The region back of the knee joint; the popliteal space; the hock.
The thigh of any animal; especially, the thigh of a hog cured by salting and smoking.
q: A plentiful lack of wit, together with most weak hams.

Ham.etym: [AS. ham; akin to D. ham, dial. G. hamme, OHG. hamma. Perh. named from the bend at the ham, and akin to E. chamber. Cf. Gammon ham.]

senses.d: An instrument for driving nails, beating metals, and the like, consisting of a head, usually of steel or iron, fixed crosswise to a handle.
q: With busy hammers closing rivets up.

senses.d: Something which in form or action resembles the common hammer
q: He met the stern legionaries who had been the “massive iron hammers” of the whole earth.

Hammer.etym: [OE. hamer, AS. hamer, hamor; akin to D. hamer, G. & Dan. hammer, Sw. hammare, Icel. hamarr, hammer, crag, and perh. to Gr. ἄκμων anvil, Skr. açman stone.]

senses.d: To beat with a hammer; to beat with heavy blows; as, to hammer iron.
To form or forge with a hammer; to shape by beating.
To form in the mind; to shape by hard intellectual labor; — usually with out.
q: Who was hammering out a penny dialogue.

senses.d: To be busy forming anything; to labor hard as if shaping something with a hammer.
q: Whereon this month I have been hammering.

senses.d: To strike repeated blows, literally or figuratively.
q: Blood and revenge are hammering in my head.

senses.d: A spherical weight attached to a flexible handle and hurled from a mark or ring. The weight of head and handle is usually not less than 16 pounds.
To have; have.
q: Him thanken all, and thus they han an end.

Han.etym: contr. inf. & plural pres. of Haven.

senses.d: That part of the fore limb below the forearm or wrist in man and monkeys, and the corresponding part in many other animals; manus; paw. See Manus.
That which resembles, or to some extent performs the office of, a human hand
A measure equal to a hand's breadth, — four inches; a palm. Chiefly used in measuring the height of horses.
Side; part; direction, either right or left.
q: On this hand and that hand, were hangings.
The Protestants were then on the winning hand.

senses.d: Power of performance; means of execution; ability; skill; dexterity.
q: He had a great mind to try his hand at a Spectator.

senses.d: Actual performance; deed; act; workmanship; agency; hence, manner of performance.
q: To change the hand in carrying on the war.
Gideon said unto God, If thou wilt save Israel by my hand.

senses.d: An agent; a servant, or laborer; a workman, trained or competent for special service or duty; a performer more or less skillful; as, a deck hand; a farm hand; an old hand at speaking.
q: A dictionary containing a natural history requires too many hands, as well as too much time, ever to be hoped for.
I was always reckoned a lively hand at a simile.

senses.d: Handwriting; style of penmanship; as, a good, bad, or running hand. Hence, a signature.
q: I say she never did invent this letter; This is a man's invention and his hand.
Some writs require a judge's hand.

senses.d: Personal possession; ownership; hence, control; direction; management; — usually in the plural.
q: Albinus . . . found means to keep in his hands the government of Britain.

senses.d: Agency in transmission from one person to another; as, to buy at first hand, that is, from the producer, or when new; at second hand, that is, when no longer in the producer's hand, or when not new.
Rate; price.
That which is, or may be, held in a hand at once

Hand.etym: [AS. hand, hond; akin to D., G., & Sw. hand, OHG. hant, Dan. haand, Icel. hönd, Goth. handus, and perh. to Goth. hinþan to seize (in comp.). Cf. Hunt.]

senses.d: To give, pass, or transmit with the hand; as, he handed them the letter.
To lead, guide, or assist with the hand; to conduct; as, to hand a lady into a carriage.
To manage; as, I hand my oar.
To seize; to lay hands on.
To pledge by the hand; to handfast.
To furl; — said of a sail.
To coöperate.
A gambling game played by American Indians, consisting of guessing the whereabouts of bits of ivory or the like, which are passed rapidly from hand to hand.
A space equal to the breadth of the hand; a palm.
With hands joined; hand in hand.
q: Into their inmost bower, Handed they went.

senses.d: Having a peculiar or characteristic hand.
q: As poisonous tongued as handed.

senses.d: As much as the hand will grasp or contain.
A hand's breadth; four inches.
q: Knap the tongs together about a handful from the bottom.

senses.d: A small quantity or number.
q: This handful of men were tied to very hard duty.
They had their handful to defend themselves from firing.

senses.d: A piece of cloth, usually square and often fine and elegant, carried for wiping the face or hands.
A piece of cloth shaped like a handkerchief to be worn about the neck; a neckerchief; a neckcloth.
To touch; to feel with the hand; to use or hold with the hand.
q: Handle me, and see; for a spirit hath not flesh.
About his altar, handling holy things.

senses.d: To manage in using, as a spade or a musket; to wield; often, to manage skillfully.
q: That fellow handles his bow like a crowkeeper.

senses.d: To accustom to the hand; to work upon, or take care of, with the hands.
q: The hardness of the winters forces the breeders to house and handle their colts six months every year.

senses.d: To receive and transfer; to have pass through one's hands; hence, to buy and sell; as, a merchant handles a variety of goods, or a large stock.
To deal with; to make a business of.
q: They that handle the law knew me not.

senses.d: To treat; to use, well or ill.
q: How wert thou handled being prisoner?

senses.d: To manage; to control; to practice skill upon.
q: You shall see how I will handle her.

senses.d: To use or manage in writing or speaking; to treat, as a theme, an argument, or an objection.
q: We will handle what persons are apt to envy others.

Handle.etym: [OE. handlen, AS. handlian; akin to D. handelen to trade, G. handeln. See Hand.]

senses.d: To use the hands.
q: They have hands, but they handle not.

senses.d: That part of vessels, instruments, etc., which is held in the hand when used or moved, as the haft of a sword, the knob of a door, the bail of a kettle, etc.
That of which use is made; the instrument for effecting a purpose; a tool.
A touching, controlling, managing, using, etc., with the hand or hands, or as with the hands. See Handle, v. t.
q: The heavens and your fair handling Have made you master of the field this day.

senses.d: The mode of using the pencil or brush, etc.; style of touch.
A maid that waits at hand; a female servant or attendant.
The cast or form of writing peculiar to each hand or person; chirography.
That which is written by hand; manuscript.
To suspend; to fasten to some elevated point without support from below; — often used with up or out; as, to hang a coat on a hook; to hang up a sign; to hang out a banner.
To fasten in a manner which will allow of free motion upon the point or points of suspension; — said of a pendulum, a swing, a door, gate, etc.
To fit properly, as at a proper angle (a part of an implement that is swung in using), as a scythe to its snath, or an ax to its helve.
To put to death by suspending by the neck; — a form of capital punishment; as, to hang a murderer.
To cover, decorate, or furnish by hanging pictures, trophies, drapery, and the like, or by covering with paper hangings; — said of a wall, a room, etc.
q: Hung be the heavens with black.
And hung thy holy roofs with savage spoils.

senses.d: To paste, as paper hangings, on the walls of a room.
To hold or bear in a suspended or inclined manner or position instead of erect; to droop; as, he hung his head in shame.
q: Cowslips wan that hang the pensive head.

Hang.etym: [OE. hangen, hongien, v. t. & i., AS. hangian, v. i., fr. hōn, v. t. (imp. heng, p. p. hongen); akin to OS. hangōn, v. i., D. hangen, v. t. & i., G. hangen, v. i., hängen, v. t., Icel. hanga, v. i., Goth. hāhan, v. t. (imp. haíhah), hāhan, v. i. (imp. hahaida), and perh. to L. cunctari to delay. √37

senses.d: To be suspended or fastened to some elevated point without support from below; to dangle; to float; to rest; to remain; to stay.
To be fastened in such a manner as to allow of free motion on the point or points of suspension.
To die or be put to death by suspension from the neck.
To hold for support; to depend; to cling; — usually with on or upon; as, this question hangs on a single point.
To be, or be like, a suspended weight.
q: Life hangs upon me, and becomes a burden.

senses.d: To hover; to impend; to appear threateningly; — usually with over; as, evils hang over the country.
To lean or incline; to incline downward.
q: To decide which way hung the victory.
His neck obliquely o'er his shoulder hung.

senses.d: To slope down; as, hanging grounds.
To be undetermined or uncertain; to be in suspense; to linger; to be delayed.
q: A noble stroke he lifted high, Which hung not, but so swift with tempest fell On the proud crest of Satan.

senses.d: The manner in which one part or thing hangs upon, or is connected with, another; as, the hang of a scythe.
Connection; arrangement; plan; as, the hang of a discourse.
A sharp or steep declivity or slope.
Of a ball: To rebound unexpectedly or unusually slowly, due to backward spin on the ball or imperfections of ground.
To prevent from reaching a decision, esp. by refusing to join in a verdict that must be unanimous; as, one obstinate juror can hang a jury.
Requiring, deserving, or foreboding death by the halter.
Suspended from above; pendent; as, hanging shelves.
Adapted for sustaining a hanging object; as, the hanging post of a gate, the post which holds the hinges.
The act of suspending anything; the state of being suspended.
Death by suspension; execution by a halter.
That which is hung as lining or drapery for the walls of a room, as tapestry, paper, etc., or to cover or drape a door or window; — used chiefly in the plural.
q: Now purple hangings clothe the palace walls.

senses.d: To clothe; to wrap.
q: The surgeon happed her up carefully.

senses.d: A cloak or plaid.
That which happens or comes suddenly or unexpectedly; also, the manner of occurrence or taking place; chance; fortune; accident; casual event; fate; luck; lot.
q: Whether art it was or heedless hap.
Cursed be good haps, and cursed be they that build Their hopes on haps.
Loving goes by haps: Some Cupid kills with arrows, some with traps.

senses.d: To happen; to befall; to chance.
q: Sends word of all that haps in Tyre.

Hap.etym: [OE. happen. See Hap chance, and cf. Happen.]

senses.d: By hap, chance, luck, or accident; perhaps; it may be.
q: Lest haply ye be found even to fight against God.

senses.d: To come by chance; to come without previous expectation; to fall out.
q: There shall no evil happen to the just.

senses.d: To take place; to occur.
q: All these things which had happened.

Happen.etym: [OE. happenen, hapnen. See Hap to happen.]

senses.d: Favored by hap, luck, or fortune; lucky; fortunate; successful; prosperous; satisfying desire; as, a happy expedient; a happy effort; a happy venture; a happy omen.
q: Chymists have been more happy in finding experiments than the causes of them.

senses.d: Experiencing the effect of favorable fortune; having the feeling arising from the consciousness of well-being or of enjoyment; enjoying good of any kind, as peace, tranquillity, comfort; contented; joyous; as, happy hours, happy thoughts.
q: Happy is that people, whose God is the Lord.
The learned is happy Nature to explore, The fool is happy that he knows no more.

senses.d: Dexterous; ready; apt; felicitous.
q: One gentleman is happy at a reply, another excels in a rejoinder.

senses.d: Not easily penetrated, cut, or separated into parts; not yielding to pressure; firm; solid; compact; — applied to material bodies, and opposed to soft; as, hard wood; hard flesh; a hard apple.
Difficult, mentally or judicially; not easily apprehended, decided, or resolved; as a hard problem.
q: The hard causes they brought unto Moses.
In which are some things hard to be understood.

senses.d: Difficult to accomplish; full of obstacles; laborious; fatiguing; arduous; as, a hard task; a disease hard to cure.
Difficult to resist or control; powerful.
q: The stag was too hard for the horse.
A power which will be always too hard for them.

senses.d: Difficult to bear or endure; not easy to put up with or consent to; hence, severe; rigorous; oppressive; distressing; unjust; grasping; as, a hard lot; hard times; hard fare; a hard winter; hard conditions or terms.
q: I never could drive a hard bargain.

senses.d: Difficult to please or influence; stern; unyielding; obdurate; unsympathetic; unfeeling; cruel; as, a hard master; a hard heart; hard words; a hard character.
Not easy or agreeable to the taste; harsh; stiff; rigid; ungraceful; repelling; as, a hard style.
q: Figures harder than even the marble itself.

senses.d: Rough; acid; sour, as liquors; as, hard cider.

Abrupt or explosive in utterance; not aspirated, sibilated, or pronounced with a gradual change of the organs from one position to another; — said of certain consonants, as c in came, and g in go, as distinguished from the same letters in center, general, etc.
Wanting softness or smoothness of utterance; harsh; as, a hard tone.
Rigid in the drawing or distribution of the figures; formal; lacking grace of composition.

Hard.syn: Solid; arduous; powerful; trying; unyielding; stubborn; stern; flinty; unfeeling; harsh; difficult; severe; obdurate; rigid. See Solid, and Arduous.
Hard.etym: [OE. hard, heard, AS. heard; akin to OS. & D. hard, G. hart, OHG. herti, harti, Icel. harðr, Dan. haard, Sw. hård, Goth. hardus, Gr. κρατύσ strong, κάρτοσ, κράτοσ, strength, and also to E. -ard, as in coward, drunkard, -crat, -cracy in autocrat, democracy; cf. Skr. kratu strength, kṛ to do, make. Cf

senses.d: With pressure; with urgency; hence, diligently; earnestly.
q: And prayed so hard for mercy from the prince.
My father Is hard at study; pray now, rest yourself.

senses.d: With difficulty; as, the vehicle moves hard.
Uneasily; vexatiously; slowly.
So as to raise difficulties.
With tension or strain of the powers; violently; with force; tempestuously; vehemently; vigorously; energetically; as, to press, to blow, to rain hard; hence, rapidly; nimbly; as, to run hard.
Close or near.
q: Whose house joined hard to the synagogue.

senses.d: To harden; to make hard.
A ford or passage across a river or swamp.
To make hard or harder; to make firm or compact; to indurate; as, to harden clay or iron.
To accustom by labor or suffering to endure with constancy; to strengthen; to stiffen; to inure; also, to confirm in wickedness or shame; to make unimpressionable.
q: I would harden myself in sorrow.

senses.d: To become hard or harder; to acquire solidity, or more compactness; as, mortar hardens by drying.
q: The deliberate judgment of those who knew him has hardened into tradition.

senses.d: To become confirmed or strengthened, in either a good or a bad sense.
q: They, hardened more by what might most reclaim.

senses.d: Made hard, or harder, or compact; made unfeeling or callous; made obstinate or obdurate; confirmed in error or vice.

Hardened.syn: Impenetrable; hard; obdurate; callous; unfeeling; unsusceptible; insensible. See Obdurate.

senses.d: A South African mullet, salted for food.
In a hard or difficult manner; with difficulty.
q: Recovering hardly what he lost before.

senses.d: Unwillingly; grudgingly.
q: The House of Peers gave so hardly their consent.

senses.d: Scarcely; barely; not quite; not wholly.
q: Hardly shall you find any one so bad, but he desires the credit of being thought good.

senses.d: Severely; harshly; roughly.
q: He has in many things been hardly used.

senses.d: Confidently; hardily.
Certainly; surely; indeed.
The quality or state of being hard, literally or figuratively.
q: The habit of authority also had given his manners some peremptory hardness.

senses.d: The cohesion of the particles on the surface of a body, determined by its capacity to scratch another, or be itself scratched; — measured among minerals on a scale of which diamond and talc form the extremes.
The peculiar quality exhibited by water which has mineral salts dissolved in it. Such water forms an insoluble compound with soap, and is hence unfit for washing purposes.
To excite; to tease, harass, or worry; to harry.
A rodent of the genus Lepus, having long hind legs, a short tail, and a divided upper lip. It is a timid animal, moves swiftly by leaps, and is remarkable for its fecundity.
A small constellation situated south of and under the foot of Orion; Lepus.

Hare.etym: [AS. hara; akin to D. haas, G. hase, OHG. haso, Dan. & Sw. hare, Icel. hēri, Skr. çaça. √226.]

senses.d: A churl; a common man; a person, male or female, of low birth.
q: He was a gentle harlot and a kind.

senses.d: A person given to low conduct; a rogue; a cheat; a rascal.
A woman who prostitutes her body for hire; a prostitute; a common woman; a strumpet.

Harlot.etym: [OE. harlot, herlot, a vagabond, OF. harlot, herlot, arlot; cf. Pr. arlot, Sp. arlote, It. arlotto; of uncertain origin.]

senses.d: Wanton; lewd; low; base.
To play the harlot; to practice lewdness.
Injury; hurt; damage; detriment; misfortune.
That which causes injury, damage, or loss.
q: We, ignorant of ourselves, Beg often our own harms.

Harm.syn: Mischief; evil; loss; injury. See Mischief.
Harm.etym: [OE. harm, hearm, AS. hearm; akin to OS. harm, G. harm grief, Icel. harmr, Dan. harme, Sw. harm; cf. OSlav. & Russ. sram' shame, Skr. çrama toil, fatigue.]

senses.d: To hurt; to injure; to damage; to wrong.
q: Though yet he never harmed me.
No ground of enmity between us known Why he should mean me ill or seek to harm.

Harm.etym: [OE. harmen, AS. hearmian. See Harm, n.]

senses.d: Free from harm; unhurt; as, to give bond to save another harmless.
Free from power or disposition to harm; innocent; inoffensive.

Harmless.syn: Innocent; innoxious; innocuous; inoffensive; unoffending; unhurt; uninjured; unharmed.

senses.d: Originally, the complete dress, especially in a military sense, of a man or a horse; hence, in general, armor.
q: At least we'll die with harness on our back.

senses.d: The equipment of a draught or carriage horse, for drawing a wagon, coach, chaise, etc.; gear; tackling.
The part of a loom comprising the heddles, with their means of support and motion, by which the threads of the warp are alternately raised and depressed for the passage of the shuttle.

Harness.etym: [OE. harneis, harnes, OF. harneis, F. harnais, harnois; of Celtic origin; cf. Armor. harnez old iron, armor, W. haiarn iron, Armor. houarn, Ir. iarann, Gael. iarunn. Cf. Iron.]

senses.d: To dress in armor; to equip with armor for war, as a horseman; to array.
q: Harnessed in rugged steel.
A gay dagger, Harnessed well and sharp as point of spear.

senses.d: Fig.: To equip or furnish for defense.
To make ready for draught; to equip with harness, as a horse. Also used figuratively.
q: Harnessed to some regular profession.

Harness.etym: [OE. harneisen; cf. F. harnacher, OF. harneschier.]

senses.d: A musical instrument consisting of a triangular frame furnished with strings and sometimes with pedals, held upright, and played with the fingers.
A constellation; Lyra, or the Lyre.
A grain sieve.

Harp.etym: [OE. harpe, AS. hearpe; akin to D. harp, G. harfe, OHG. harpha, Dan. harpe, Icel. & Sw. harpa.]

senses.d: To play on the harp.
q: I heard the voice of harpers, harping with their harps.

senses.d: To dwell on or recur to a subject tediously or monotonously in speaking or in writing; to refer to something repeatedly or continually; — usually with on or upon.
q: Harping on what I am, Not what he knew I was.

senses.d: To play on, as a harp; to play (a tune) on the harp; to develop or give expression to by skill and art; to sound forth as from a harp; to hit upon.
q: Thou 'st harped my fear aright.

senses.d: A player on the harp; a minstrel.
q: The murmuring pines and the hemlocks . . . Stand like harpers hoar, with beards that rest on their bosoms.

senses.d: A brass coin bearing the emblem of a harp, — formerly current in Ireland.
Pertaining to the harp; as, harping symphonies.

An implement of agriculture, usually formed of pieces of timber or metal crossing each other, and set with iron or wooden teeth. It is drawn over plowed land to level it and break the clods, to stir the soil and make it fine, or to cover seed when sown.
An obstacle formed by turning an ordinary harrow upside down, the frame being buried.

Harrow.etym: [OE. harowe, harwe, AS. hearge; cf. D. hark rake, G. harke, Icel. herfi harrow, Dan. harve, Sw. harf. √16.]

senses.d: To draw a harrow over, as for the purpose of breaking clods and leveling the surface, or for covering seed; as, to harrow land.
q: Will he harrow the valleys after thee?

senses.d: To break or tear, as with a harrow; to wound; to lacerate; to torment or distress; to vex.
q: My aged muscles harrowed up with whips.
I could a tale unfold, whose lightest word Would harrow up thy soul.

Harrow.etym: [OE. harowen, harwen; cf. Dan. harve. See Harrow, n.]

senses.d: Help! Halloo! An exclamation of distress; a call for succor; — the ancient Norman hue and cry.
q: Harrow! alas! here lies my fellow slain.

Harrow.etym: [OF. harau, haro; fr. OHG. hara, hera, herot, or fr. OS. herod hither, akin to E. here.]

senses.d: To pillage; to harry; to oppress.
q: Meaning thereby to harrow his people.

senses.d: A stag; the male of the red deer. See the Note under Buck.
q: Goodliest of all the forest, hart and hind.

Hart.etym: [OE. hart, hert, heort, AS. heort, heorot; akin to D. hert, OHG. hiruz, hirz, G. hirsch, Icel. hjörtr, Dan. & Sw. hjort, L. cervus, and prob. to Gr. κεραόσ horned, κέρασ horn. √230. See Horn.]

senses.d: The gathering of a crop of any kind; the ingathering of the crops; also, the season of gathering grain and fruits, late summer or early autumn.
q: Seedtime and harvest . . . shall not cease.
At harvest, when corn is ripe.

senses.d: That which is reaped or ready to be reaped or gathered; a crop, as of grain (wheat, maize, etc.), or fruit.
q: Put ye in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe.
To glean the broken ears after the man That the main harvest reaps.

senses.d: The product or result of any exertion or labor; gain; reward.
q: The pope's principal harvest was in the jubilee.
The harvest of a quiet eye.

Harvest.etym: [OE. harvest, hervest, AS. hærfest autumn; akin to LG. harfst, D. herfst, OHG. herbist, G. herbst, and prob. to L. carpere to pluck, Gr. καρπόσ fruit. Cf. Carpet.]

senses.d: To reap or gather, as any crop.
A man engaged in harvesting.
That which is hashed or chopped up; meat and vegetables, especially such as have been already cooked, chopped into small pieces and mixed.
A new mixture of old matter; a second preparation or exhibition.
q: I can not bear elections, and still less the hash of them over again in a first session.

Hash.etym: [Formerly hachey, hachee, F. hachis, fr. hacher to hash; of German origin; cf. G. hippe sickle, OHG. hippa, for happia. Cf. Hatchet.]

senses.d: To chop into small pieces; to mince and mix; as, to hash meat.

Hash.etym: [From Hash, n.: cf. F. hacher to hash.]

senses.d: Celerity of motion; speed; swiftness; dispatch; expedition; — applied only to voluntary beings, as men and other animals.
q: The king's business required haste.

senses.d: The state of being urged or pressed by business; hurry; urgency; sudden excitement of feeling or passion; precipitance; vehemence.
q: I said in my haste, All men are liars.

Haste.syn: Speed; quickness; nimbleness; swiftness; expedition; dispatch; hurry; precipitance; vehemence; precipitation.
Haste.etym: [OE. hast; akin to D. haast, G., Dan., Sw., & OFries. hast, cf. OF. haste, F. hâte (of German origin); all perh. fr. the root of E. hate in a earlier sense of, to pursue. See Hate.]

senses.d: To hasten; to hurry.
q: I 'll haste the writer.
They were troubled and hasted away.

Haste.etym: [OE. hasten; akin to G. hasten, D. haasten, Dan. haste, Sw. hasta, OF. haster, F. hâter. See Haste, n.]

senses.d: To press; to drive or urge forward; to push on; to precipitate; to accelerate the movement of; to expedite; to hurry.
q: I would hasten my escape from the windy storm.

senses.d: To move with celerity; to be rapid in motion; to act speedily or quickly; to go quickly.
q: I hastened to the spot whence the noise came.

senses.d: In haste; with speed or quickness; speedily; nimbly.
Without due reflection; precipitately; rashly.
q: We hastily engaged in the war.

senses.d: Passionately; impatiently.
Involving haste; done, made, etc., in haste; as, a hasty retreat; a hasty sketch.
Demanding haste or immediate action.
Moving or acting with haste or in a hurry; hurrying; hence, acting without deliberation; precipitate; rash; easily excited; eager.
q: Seest thou a man that is hasty in his words? There is more hope of a fool than of him.
The hasty multitude Admiring entered.
Be not hasty to go out of his sight.

senses.d: Made or reached without deliberation or due caution; as, a hasty conjecture, inference, conclusion, etc., a hasty resolution.
Proceeding from, or indicating, a quick temper.
q: Take no unkindness of his hasty words.

senses.d: Forward; early; first ripe.

Hasty.etym: [Akin to D. haastig, G., Sw., & Dan. hastig. See Haste, n.]

senses.d: Hot.
A covering for the head; esp., one with a crown and brim, made of various materials, and worn by men or women for protecting the head from the sun or weather, or for ornament.

Hat.etym: [AS. hæt, hætt; akin to Dan. hat, Sw. hatt, Icel. hattr a hat, höttr hood, D. hoed hat, G. hut, OHG. huot, and prob. to L. cassis helmet. √13. Cf. Hood.]

senses.d: To cross with lines in a peculiar manner in drawing and engraving. See Hatching.
q: Shall win this sword, silvered and hatched.
Those hatching strokes of the pencil.

senses.d: To cross; to spot; to stain; to steep.
q: His weapon hatched in blood.

Hatch.etym: [F. hacher to chop, hack. See Hash.]

senses.d: To produce, as young, from an egg or eggs by incubation, or by artificial heat; to produce young from (eggs); as, the young when hatched.
q: As the partridge sitteth on eggs, and hatcheth them not.
For the hens do not sit upon the eggs; but by keeping them in a certain equal heat they bring life into them and hatch them.

senses.d: To contrive or plot; to form by meditation, and bring into being; to originate and produce; to concoct; as, to hatch mischief; to hatch heresy.
q: Fancies hatched In silken-folded idleness.

Hatch.etym: [OE. hacchen, hetchen; akin to G. hecken, Dan. hekke; cf. MHG. hagen bull; perh. akin to E. hatch a half door, and orig. meaning, to produce under a hatch. √12.]

senses.d: To produce young; — said of eggs; to come forth from the egg; — said of the young of birds, fishes, insects, etc.
The act of hatching.
Development; disclosure; discovery.
The chickens produced at once or by one incubation; a brood.
A door with an opening over it; a half door, sometimes set with spikes on the upper edge.
q: In at the window, or else o'er the hatch.

senses.d: A frame or weir in a river, for catching fish.
A flood gate; a sluice gate.
A bedstead.
An opening in the deck of a vessel or floor of a warehouse which serves as a passageway or hoistway; a hatchway; also; a cover or door, or one of the covers used in closing such an opening.
An opening into, or in search of, a mine.

Hatch.etym: [OE. hacche, AS. hæc, cf. haca the bar of a door, D. hek gate, Sw. häck coop, rack, Dan. hekke manger, rack. Prob. akin to E. hook, and first used of something made of pieces fastened together. Cf. Heck, Hack a frame.]

senses.d: To close with a hatch or hatches.
q: 'T were not amiss to keep our door hatched.

senses.d: To have a great aversion to, with a strong desire that evil should befall the person toward whom the feeling is directed; to dislike intensely; to detest; as, to hate one's enemies; to hate hypocrisy.
q: Whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer.

senses.d: To be very unwilling; followed by an infinitive, or a substantive clause with that; as, to hate to get into debt; to hate that anything should be wasted.
q: I hate that he should linger here.

senses.d: To love less, relatively.

Hate.syn: To Hate, Abhor, Detest, Abominate, Loathe.
Hate.etym: [OE. haten, hatien, AS. hatian; akin to OS. hatan, hatōn to be hostile to, D. haten to hate, OHG. hazzēn, hazzōn, G. hassen, Icel. & Sw. hata, Dan. hade, Goth. hatan, hatjan. √36. Cf. Hate, n., Heinous.]

senses.d: Strong aversion coupled with desire that evil should befall the person toward whom the feeling is directed; as exercised toward things, intense dislike; hatred; detestation; — opposed to love.
q: For in a wink the false love turns to hate.

Hate.etym: [OE. hate, hete, AS. hete; akin to D. haat, G. hass, Icel. hatr, SW. hat, Dan. had, Goth. hatis. Cf. Hate, v.]

senses.d: Manifesting hate or hatred; malignant; malevolent.
q: And worse than death, to view with hateful eyes His rival's conquest.

senses.d: Exciting or deserving great dislike, aversion, or disgust; odious.
q: Unhappy, wretched, hateful day!

Hateful.syn: Odious; detestable; abominable; execrable; loathsome; abhorrent; repugnant; malevolent.

senses.d: One who hates.
q: An enemy to God, and a hater of all good.

senses.d: Has.
Strong aversion; intense dislike; hate; an affection of the mind awakened by something regarded as evil.

Hatred.syn: Odium; ill will; enmity; hate; animosity; malevolence; rancor; malignity; detestation; loathing; abhorrence; repugnance; antipathy. See Odium.
Hatred.etym: [OE. hatred, hatreden. See Hate, and cf. Kindred.]

senses.d: In a haughty manner; arrogantly.
The quality of being haughty; disdain; arrogance.
High; lofty; bold.
q: To measure the most haughty mountain's height.
Equal unto this haughty enterprise.

senses.d: Disdainfully or contemptuously proud; arrogant; overbearing.
q: A woman of a haughty and imperious nature.

senses.d: Indicating haughtiness; as, a haughty carriage.
q: Satan, with vast and haughty strides advanced, Came towering.

Haughty.etym: [OE. hautein, F. hautain, fr. haut high, OF. also halt, fr. L. altus. See Altitude.]

senses.d: To frequent; to resort to frequently; to visit pertinaciously or intrusively; to intrude upon.
q: You wrong me, sir, thus still to haunt my house.
Those cares that haunt the court and town.

senses.d: To inhabit or frequent as a specter; to visit as a ghost or apparition.
q: Foul spirits haunt my resting place.

senses.d: To practice; to devote one's self to.
q: That other merchandise that men haunt with fraud . . . is cursed.
Leave honest pleasure, and haunt no good pastime.

senses.d: To accustom; to habituate.
q: Haunt thyself to pity.

Haunt.etym: [F. hanter; of uncertain origin, perh. from an assumed LL. ambitare to go about, fr. L. ambire (see Ambition); or cf. Icel. heimta to demand, regain, akin to heim home (see Home). √36.]

senses.d: To persist in staying or visiting.
q: I've charged thee not to haunt about my doors.

senses.d: A place to which one frequently resorts; as, drinking saloons are the haunts of tipplers; a den is the haunt of wild beasts.
q: The household nook, The haunt of all affections pure.
The feeble soul, a haunt of fears.

senses.d: The habit of resorting to a place.
q: The haunt you have got about the courts.

senses.d: Practice; skill.
q: Of clothmaking she hadde such an haunt.

senses.d: To hold in possession or control; to own; as, he has a farm.
To possess, as something which appertains to, is connected with, or affects, one.
q: The earth hath bubbles, as the water has.
He had a fever late.

senses.d: To accept possession of; to take or accept.
q: Break thy mind to me in broken English; wilt thou have me?

senses.d: To get possession of; to obtain; to get.
To cause or procure to be; to effect; to exact; to desire; to require.
q: I had the church accurately described to me.
Wouldst thou have me turn traitor also?

senses.d: To bear, as young; as, she has just had a child.
To hold, regard, or esteem.
q: Of them shall I be had in honor.

senses.d: To cause or force to go; to take.

To take or hold (one's self); to proceed promptly; — used reflexively, often with ellipsis of the pronoun; as, to have after one; to have at one or at a thing, i.e., to aim at one or at a thing; to attack; to have with a companion.
To be under necessity or obligation; to be compelled; followed by an infinitive.
q: Science has, and will long have, to be a divider and a separatist.
The laws of philology have to be established by external comparison and induction.

senses.d: To understand.
q: You have me, have you not?

senses.d: To put in an awkward position; to have the advantage of; as, that is where he had him.
q: Myself for such a face had boldly died.

Have.syn: To possess; to own. See Possess.
Have.etym: [OE. haven, habben, AS. habben (imperf. hæfde, p. p. gehæfd); akin to OS. hebbian, D. hebben, OFries. hebba, OHG. habēn, G. haben, Icel. hafa, Sw. hafva, Dan. have, Goth. haban, and prob. to L. habere, whence F. avoir. Cf. Able, Avoirdupois, Binnacle, Habit.]

senses.d: A bay, recess, or inlet of the sea, or the mouth of a river, which affords anchorage and shelter for shipping; a harbor; a port.
q: What shipping and what lading 's in our haven.
Their haven under the hill.

senses.d: A place of safety; a shelter; an asylum.
q: The haven, or the rock of love.

Haven.etym: [AS. hæfene; akin to D. & LG. haven, G. hafen, MHG. habe, Dan. havn, Icel. höfn, Sw. hamn; akin to E. have, and hence orig., a holder; or to heave (see Heave); or akin to AS. hæf sea, Icel. & Sw. haf, Dan. hav, which is perh. akin to E. heave.]

senses.d: To shelter, as in a haven.
Possession; goods; estate.
q: I 'll lend you something; my having is not much.

senses.d: One of numerous species and genera of rapacious birds of the family Falconidæ. They differ from the true falcons in lacking the prominent tooth and notch of the bill, and in having shorter and less pointed wings. Many are of large size and grade into the eagles. Some, as the goshawk, were formerly trained like falcons. In a more general sense the word is not infrequently applied, also, to true falcons, as the sparrow hawk, pigeon hawk, duck hawk, and prairie hawk.

Hawk.etym: [OE. hauk (prob. fr. Icel.), havek, AS. hafoc, heafoc; akin to D. havik, OHG. habuh, G. habicht, Icel. haukr, Sw. hök, Dan. hög, prob. from the root of E. heave.]

senses.d: To catch, or attempt to catch, birds by means of hawks trained for the purpose, and let loose on the prey; to practice falconry.
q: A falconer Henry is, when Emma hawks.

senses.d: To make an attack while on the wing; to soar and strike like a hawk; — generally with at; as, to hawk at flies.
q: A falcon, towering in her pride of place, Was by a mousing owl hawked at and killed.

senses.d: To clear the throat with an audible sound by forcing an expiratory current of air through the narrow passage between the depressed soft palate and the root of the tongue, thus aiding in the removal of foreign substances.
To raise by hawking, as phlegm.
An effort to force up phlegm from the throat, accompanied with noise.
To offer for sale by outcry in the street; to carry (merchandise) about from place to place for sale; to peddle; as, to hawk goods or pamphlets.
q: His works were hawked in every street.

Hawk.etym: [Akin to D. hauker a hawker, G. höken, höcken, to higgle, to retail, höke, höker, a higgler, huckster. See Huckster.]

senses.d: A small board, with a handle on the under side, to hold mortar.
A hedge.
A net set around the haunt of an animal, especially of a rabbit.

Hay.etym: [AS. hege: cf. F. haie, of German origin. See Haw a hedge, Hedge.]

senses.d: To lay snares for rabbits.
Grass cut and cured for fodder.
q: Make hay while the sun shines.
Hay may be dried too much as well as too little.

Hay.etym: [OE. hei, AS. hēg; akin to D. hooi, OHG. hewi, houwi, G. heu, Dan. & Sw. hö, Icel. hey, ha, Goth. hawi grass, fr. the root of E. hew. See Hew to cut.]

senses.d: To cut and cure grass for hay.
A game of chance played with dice.
The uncertain result of throwing a die; hence, a fortuitous event; chance; accident; casualty.
q: I will stand the hazard of the die.

senses.d: Risk; danger; peril; as, he encountered the enemy at the hazard of his reputation and life.
q: Men are led on from one stage of life to another in a condition of the utmost hazard.

senses.d: Holing a ball, whether the object ball (winning hazard) or the player's ball (losing hazard).
Anything that is hazarded or risked, as the stakes in gaming.

Hazard.etym: [F. hasard, Sp. azar an unforeseen disaster or accident, an unfortunate card or throw at dice, prob. fr. Ar. zahr, zār, a die, which, with the article al the, would give azzahr, azzār.]

senses.d: To expose to the operation of chance; to put in danger of loss or injury; to venture; to risk.
q: Men hazard nothing by a course of evangelical obedience.
He hazards his neck to the halter.

senses.d: To venture to incur, or bring on.
q: I hazarded the loss of whom I loved.
They hazard to cut their feet.

Hazard.syn: To venture; risk; jeopard; peril; endanger.

senses.d: To try the chance; to encounter risk or danger.
Any place into which the ball may not be safely played, such as bunkers, furze, water, sand, or other kind of bad ground.

A shrub or small tree of the genus Corylus, as the C. avellana, bearing a nut containing a kernel of a mild, farinaceous taste; the filbert. The American species are C. Americana, which produces the common hazelnut, and C. rostrata. See Filbert.
A miner's name for freestone.

Hazel.etym: [OE. hasel, AS. hæsel; akin to D. hazelaar, G. hazel, OHG. hasal, hasala, Icel. hasl, Dan & Sw. hassel, L. corylus, for cosylus.]

senses.d: Consisting of hazels, or of the wood of the hazel; pertaining to, or derived from, the hazel; as, a hazel wand.
q: I sit me down beside the hazel grove.

senses.d: Of a light brown color, like the hazelnut.

The man or male being (or object personified to which the masculine gender is assigned), previously designated; a pronoun of the masculine gender, usually referring to a specified subject already indicated.
q: Thy desire shall be to thy husband, and he shall rule over thee.
Thou shalt fear the Lord thy God; him shalt thou serve.

senses.d: Any one; the man or person; — used indefinitely, and usually followed by a relative pronoun.
q: He that walketh with wise men shall be wise.

senses.d: Man; a male; any male person; — in this sense used substantively.
q: I stand to answer thee, Or any he, the proudest of thy sort.

He.etym: [AS. hē, masc., heó, fem., hit, neut.; pl. hī, or hie, hig; akin to OFries. hi, D. hij, OS. he, hi, G. heute to-day, Goth. himma, dat. masc., this, hina, accus. masc., and hita, accus. neut., and prob. to L. hic this. √183. Cf. It.]

senses.d: The anterior or superior part of an animal, containing the brain, or chief ganglia of the nervous system, the mouth, and in the higher animals, the chief sensory organs; poll; cephalon.

The uppermost, foremost, or most important part of an inanimate object; such a part as may be considered to resemble the head of an animal; often, also, the larger, thicker, or heavier part or extremity, in distinction from the smaller or thinner part, or from the point or edge; as, the head of a cane, a nail, a spear, an ax, a mast, a sail, a ship; that which covers and closes the top or the end of a hollow vessel; as, the head of a cask or a steam boiler.
The place where the head should go; as, the head of a bed, of a grave, etc.; the head of a carriage, that is, the hood which covers the head.
The most prominent or important member of any organized body; the chief; the leader; as, the head of a college, a school, a church, a state, and the like.
q: The heads of the chief sects of philosophy.
Your head I him appoint.

senses.d: The place or honor, or of command; the most important or foremost position; the front; as, the head of the table; the head of a column of soldiers.
q: An army of fourscore thousand troops, with the duke of Marlborough at the head of them.

senses.d: Each one among many; an individual; — often used in a plural sense; as, a thousand head of cattle.
q: It there be six millions of people, there are about four acres for every head.

senses.d: The seat of the intellect; the brain; the understanding; the mental faculties; as, a good head, that is, a good mind; it never entered his head, it did not occur to him; of his own head, of his own thought or will.
q: Men who had lost both head and heart.

senses.d: The source, fountain, spring, or beginning, as of a stream or river; as, the head of the Nile; hence, the altitude of the source, or the height of the surface, as of water, above a given place, as above an orifice at which it issues, and the pressure resulting from the height or from motion; sometimes also, the quantity in reserve; as, a mill or reservoir has a good head of water, or ten feet head; also, that part of a gulf or bay most remote from the outlet or the sea.
A headland; a promontory; as, Gay Head.
A separate part, or topic, of a discourse; a theme to be expanded; a subdivision; as, the heads of a sermon.
Culminating point or crisis; hence, strength; force; height.
q: Ere foul sin, gathering head, shall break into corruption.
The indisposition which has long hung upon me, is at last grown to such a head, that it must quickly make an end of me or of itself.

senses.d: Power; armed force.
q: My lord, my lord, the French have gathered head.

Head.etym: [OE. hed, heved, heaved, AS. heáfod; akin to D. hoofd, OHG. houbit, G. haupt, Icel. höfuð, Sw. hufvud, Dan. hoved, Goth. haubiþ. The word does not correspond regularly to L. caput head (cf. E. Chief, Cadet, Capital), and its origin is unknown.]

senses.d: Principal; chief; leading; first; as, the head master of a school; the head man of a tribe; a head chorister; a head cook.
To be at the head of; to put one's self at the head of; to lead; to direct; to act as leader to; as, to head an army, an expedition, or a riot.
To form a head to; to fit or furnish with a head; as, to head a nail.
To behead; to decapitate.
To cut off the top of; to lop off; as, to head trees.
To go in front of; to get in the front of, so as to hinder or stop; to oppose; hence, to check or restrain; as, to head a drove of cattle; to head a person; the wind heads a ship.
To set on the head; as, to head a cask.
To originate; to spring; to have its source, as a river.
q: A broad river, that heads in the great Blue Ridge.

senses.d: To go or point in a certain direction; to tend; as, how does the ship head?
To form a head; as, this kind of cabbage heads early.
A fillet; a band for the head.
The band at each end of the back of a book.
With the head foremost; as, to fall headlong.
Rashly; precipitately; without deliberation.
Hastily; without delay or respite.

Headlong.etym: [OE. hedling, hevedlynge; prob. confused with E. long, a. & adv.]

senses.d: Rash; precipitate; as, headlong folly.
Steep; precipitous.
q: Like a tower upon a headlong rock.

senses.d: The principal stone in a foundation; the chief or corner stone.
The stone at the head of a grave.
Willful; rash; precipitate; hurried on by will or passion; ungovernable.
q: All the talent required is to be hot, to be heady, — to be violent on one side or the other.

senses.d: Apt to affect the head; intoxicating; strong.
q: The liquor is too heady.

senses.d: Violent; impetuous.
To cover, as a roof, with tiles, slate, lead, or the like.
To make hale, sound, or whole; to cure of a disease, wound, or other derangement; to restore to soundness or health.
q: Speak the word only, and my servant shall be healed.

senses.d: To remove or subdue; to cause to pass away; to cure; — said of a disease or a wound.
q: I will heal their backsliding.

senses.d: To restore to original purity or integrity.
q: Thus saith the Lord, I have healed these waters.

senses.d: To reconcile, as a breach or difference; to make whole; to free from guilt; as, to heal dissensions.

Heal.etym: [OE. helen, hælen, AS. hǣlan, fr. hāl hale, sound, whole; akin to OS. hēlian, D. heelen, G. heilen, Goth. hailjan. See Whole.]

senses.d: To grow sound; to return to a sound state; as, the limb heals, or the wound heals; — sometimes with up or over; as, it will heal up, or over.
q: Those wounds heal ill that men do give themselves.

senses.d: Health.

Heal.etym: [AS. hǣlu, hǣl. See Heal, v. t.]

senses.d: One who, or that which, heals.
Tending to cure; soothing; mollifying; as, the healing art; a healing salve; healing words.
q: Here healing dews and balms abound.

senses.d: The state of being hale, sound, or whole, in body, mind, or soul; especially, the state of being free from physical disease or pain.
q: There is no health in us.
Though health may be enjoyed without gratitude, it can not be sported with without loss, or regained by courage.

senses.d: A wish of health and happiness, as in pledging a person in a toast.

Health.etym: [OE. helthe, AS. hǣlþ, fr. hāl hale, sound, whole. See Whole.]

senses.d: A crowd; a throng; a multitude or great number of persons.
q: The wisdom of a heap of learned men.
A heap of vassals and slaves.
He had heaps of friends.

senses.d: A great number or large quantity of things not placed in a pile.
q: A vast heap, both of places of scripture and quotations.
I have noticed a heap of things in my life.

senses.d: A pile or mass; a collection of things laid in a body, or thrown together so as to form an elevation; as, a heap of earth or stones.
q: Huge heaps of slain around the body rise.

Heap.etym: [OE. heep, heap, heap, multitude, AS. heáp; akin to OS. hōp, D. hoop, OHG. houf, hūfo, G. haufe, haufen, Sw. hop, Dan. hob, Icel. hōpr troop, flock, Russ. kupa heap, crowd, Lith. kaupas. Cf. Hope, in Forlorn hope.]

senses.d: To collect in great quantity; to amass; to lay up; to accumulate; — usually with up; as, to heap up treasures.
q: Though he heap up silver as the dust.

senses.d: To throw or lay in a heap; to make a heap of; to pile; as, to heap stones; — often with up; as, to heap up earth; or with on; as, to heap on wood or coal.
To form or round into a heap, as in measuring; to fill (a measure) more than even full.
To perceive by the ear; to apprehend or take cognizance of by the ear; as, to hear sounds; to hear a voice; to hear one call.
q: Lay thine ear close to the ground, and list if thou canst hear the tread of travelers.
He had been heard to utter an ominous growl.

senses.d: To give audience or attention to; to listen to; to heed; to accept the doctrines or advice of; to obey; to examine; to try in a judicial court; as, to hear a recitation; to hear a class; the case will be heard to-morrow.
To attend, or be present at, as hearer or worshiper; as, to hear a concert; to hear Mass.
To give attention to as a teacher or judge.
q: Thy matters are good and right, but there is no man deputed of the king to hear thee.
I beseech your honor to hear me one single word.

senses.d: To accede to the demand or wishes of; to listen to and answer favorably; to favor.
q: I love the Lord, because he hath heard my voice.
They think that they shall be heard for their much speaking.

Hear.etym: [OE. heren, AS,. hiéran, hȳran, hēran; akin to OS. hōrian, OFries. hera, hora, D. hooren, OHG. hōren, G. hören, Icel. heyra, Sw. höra, Dan. hore, Goth. hausjan, and perh. to Gr. ακοὔειν, E. acoustic. Cf. Hark, Hearken.]

senses.d: To have the sense or faculty of perceiving sound.
To use the power of perceiving sound; to perceive or apprehend by the ear; to attend; to listen.
q: So spake our mother Eve, and Adam heard, Well pleased, but answered not.

senses.d: To be informed by oral communication; to be told; to receive information by report or by letter.
q: I have heard, sir, of such a man.
I must hear from thee every day in the hour.
Not only within his own camp, but also now at Rome, he heard ill for his temporizing and slow proceedings.
Hear him, . . . a cry indicative, according to the tone, of admiration, acquiescence, indignation, or derision.

senses.d: One who hears; an auditor.
The act or power of perceiving sound; perception of sound; the faculty or sense by which sound is perceived; as, my hearing is good.
q: I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear.

senses.d: Attention to what is delivered; opportunity to be heard; audience; as, I could not obtain a hearing.
A listening to facts and evidence, for the sake of adjudication; a session of a court for considering proofs and determining issues.
q: His last offenses to us Shall have judicious hearing.
Another hearing before some other court.

senses.d: Extent within which sound may be heard; sound; earshot.
q: They laid him by the pleasant shore, And in the hearing of the wave.

senses.d: To listen; to lend the ear; to attend to what is uttered; to give heed; to hear, in order to obey or comply.
q: The Furies hearken, and their snakes uncurl.
Hearken, O Israel, unto the statutes and unto the judgments, which I teach you.

senses.d: To inquire; to seek information.

Hearken.syn: To attend; listen; hear; heed. See Attend, v. i.
Hearken.etym: [OE. hercnen, hercnien, AS. hercnian, heorcnian, fr. hiéran, hȳran, to hear; akin to OD. harcken, horcken, LG. harken, horken, G. horchen. See Hear, and cf. Hark.]

senses.d: To hear by listening.
q: hearkened now and then Some little whispering and soft groaning sound.

senses.d: To give heed to; to hear attentively.
q: The King of Naples . . . hearkens my brother's suit.
If you find none, you must hearken out a vein and buy.

senses.d: A hollow, muscular organ, which, by contracting rhythmically, keeps up the circulation of the blood.
q: Why does my blood thus muster to my heart!

senses.d: The seat of the affections or sensibilities, collectively or separately, as love, hate, joy, grief, courage, and the like; rarely, the seat of the understanding or will; — usually in a good sense, when no epithet is expressed; the better or lovelier part of our nature; the spring of all our actions and purposes; the seat of moral life and character; the moral affections and character itself; the individual disposition and character; as, a good, tender, loving, bad, hard, or selfish heart.
q: Hearts are dust, hearts' loves remain.

senses.d: The nearest the middle or center; the part most hidden and within; the inmost or most essential part of any body or system; the source of life and motion in any organization; the chief or vital portion; the center of activity, or of energetic or efficient action; as, the heart of a country, of a tree, etc.
q: Exploits done in the heart of France.
Peace subsisting at the heart Of endless agitation.

senses.d: Courage; courageous purpose; spirit.
q: Eve, recovering heart, replied.
The expelled nations take heart, and when they fly from one country invade another.

senses.d: Vigorous and efficient activity; power of fertile production; condition of the soil, whether good or bad.
q: That the spent earth may gather heart again.

senses.d: That which resembles a heart in shape; especially, a roundish or oval figure or object having an obtuse point at one end, and at the other a corresponding indentation, — used as a symbol or representative of the heart.
One of a series of playing cards, distinguished by the figure or figures of a heart; as, hearts are trumps.
Vital part; secret meaning; real intention.
q: And then show you the heart of my message.

senses.d: A term of affectionate or kindly and familiar address.
q: The Lord hath sought him a man after his own heart.

Heart.etym: [OE. harte, herte, heorte, AS. heorte; akin to OS. herta, OFies. hirte, D. hart, OHG. herza, G. herz, Icel. hjarta, Sw. hjerta, Goth. haírtō, Lith. szirdis, Russ. serdtse, Ir. cridhe, L. cor, Gr. καρδία, κη̑ρ √227. Cf. Accord, Discord, Cordial, 4th Core, Courage.]

senses.d: To give heart to; to hearten; to encourage; to inspirit.
q: My cause is hearted; thine hath no less reason.

senses.d: To form a compact center or heart; as, a hearting cabbage.
Having a heart; having (such) a heart (regarded as the seat of the affections, disposition, or character).
Shaped like a heart; cordate.
Seated or laid up in the heart.
q: I hate the Moor: my cause is hearted.

senses.d: The pavement or floor of brick, stone, or metal in a chimney, on which a fire is made; the floor of a fireplace; also, a corresponding part of a stove.
q: There was a fire on the hearth burning before him.
Where fires thou find'st unraked and hearths unswept. There pinch the maids as blue as bilberry.

senses.d: The house itself, as the abode of comfort to its inmates and of hospitality to strangers; fireside.
q: Household talk and phrases of the hearth.

senses.d: The floor of a furnace, on which the material to be heated lies, or the lowest part of a melting furnace, into which the melted material settles.
q: He had been importuned by the common people to relieve them from the . . . burden of the hearth money.

Hearth.etym: [OE. harthe, herth, herthe, AS. heorð; akin to D. haard, heerd, Sw. härd, G. herd; cf. Goth. haúri a coal, Icel. hyrr embers, and L. cremare to burn.]

senses.d: From the heart; with all the heart; with sincerity.
q: I heartily forgive them.

senses.d: With zeal; actively; vigorously; willingly; cordially; as, he heartily assisted the prince.

Heartily.syn: Sincerely; cordially; zealously; vigorously; actively; warmly; eagerly; ardently; earnestly.

senses.d: Pertaining to, or proceeding from, the heart; warm; cordial; bold; zealous; sincere; willing; also, energetic; active; eager; as, a hearty welcome; hearty in supporting the government.
q: Full of hearty tears For our good father's loss.

senses.d: Exhibiting strength; sound; healthy; firm; not weak; as, a hearty man; hearty timber.
Promoting strength; nourishing; rich; abundant; as, hearty food; a hearty meal.

Hearty.syn: Sincere; real; unfeigned; undissembled; cordial; earnest; warm; zealous; ardent; eager; active; vigorous.

senses.d: Comrade; boon companion; good fellow; — a term of familiar address and fellowship among sailors.

A force in nature which is recognized in various effects, but especially in the phenomena of fusion and evaporation, and which, as manifested in fire, the sun's rays, mechanical action, chemical combination, etc., becomes directly known to us through the sense of feeling. In its nature heat is a mode of motion, being in general a form of molecular disturbance or vibration. It was formerly supposed to be a subtile, imponderable fluid, to which was given the name caloric.

The sensation caused by the force or influence of heat when excessive, or above that which is normal to the human body; the bodily feeling experienced on exposure to fire, the sun's rays, etc.; the reverse of cold.
High temperature, as distinguished from low temperature, or cold; as, the heat of summer and the cold of winter; heat of the skin or body in fever, etc.
q: Else how had the world . . . Avoided pinching cold and scorching heat!

senses.d: Indication of high temperature; appearance, condition, or color of a body, as indicating its temperature; redness; high color; flush; degree of temperature to which something is heated, as indicated by appearance, condition, or otherwise.
q: It has raised . . . heats in their faces.
The heats smiths take of their iron are a blood-red heat, a white-flame heat, and a sparkling or welding heat.

senses.d: A single complete operation of heating, as at a forge or in a furnace; as, to make a horseshoe in a certain number of heats.
A violent action unintermitted; a single effort; a single course in a race that consists of two or more courses; as, he won two heats out of three.
q: Many causes . . . for refreshment betwixt the heats.
struck off at one heat the matchless tale of “Tam o' Shanter.”

senses.d: Utmost violence; rage; vehemence; as, the heat of battle or party.
Agitation of mind; inflammation or excitement; exasperation.
Animation, as in discourse; ardor; fervency.
q: With all the strength and heat of eloquence.

senses.d: Sexual excitement in animals.
Fermentation.

Heat.etym: [OE. hete, hæte, AS. hǣtu, hǣto, fr. hāt hot; akin to OHG. heizi heat, Dan. hede, Sw. hetta. See Hot.]

senses.d: To make hot; to communicate heat to, or cause to grow warm; as, to heat an oven or furnace, an iron, or the like.
q: Heat me these irons hot.

senses.d: To excite or make hot by action or emotion; to make feverish.
q: Pray, walk softly; do not heat your blood.

senses.d: To excite ardor in; to rouse to action; to excite to excess; to inflame, as the passions.
q: A noble emulation heats your breast.

Heat.etym: [OE. heten, AS. hǣtan, fr. hāt hot. See Hot.]

senses.d: To grow warm or hot by the action of fire or friction, etc., or the communication of heat; as, the iron or the water heats slowly.
To grow warm or hot by fermentation, or the development of heat by chemical action; as, green hay heats in a mow, and manure in the dunghill.
Heated; as, the iron though heat red-hot.

A low shrub (Erica, or Calluna, vulgaris), with minute evergreen leaves, and handsome clusters of pink flowers. It is used in Great Britain for brooms, thatch, beds for the poor, and for heating ovens. It is also called heather, and ling.
A place overgrown with heath; any cheerless tract of country overgrown with shrubs or coarse herbage.
q: Their stately growth, though bare, Stands on the blasted heath.

Heath.etym: [OE. heth waste land, the plant heath, AS. hǣð; akin to D. & G. heide, Icel. heiðr waste land, Dan. hede, Sw. hed, Goth. haiþi field, L. bucetum a cow pasture; cf. W. coed a wood, Skr. kshētra field. √20.]

senses.d: An individual of the pagan or unbelieving nations, or those which worship idols and do not acknowledge the true God; a pagan; an idolater.
An irreligious person.
q: If it is no more than a moral discourse, he may preach it and they may hear it, and yet both continue unconverted heathens.
Ask of me, and I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance.

Heathen.etym: [OE. hethen, AS. hǣðen, prop. an adj. fr. hǣð heath, and orig., therefore, one who lives in the country or on the heaths and in the woods (cf. pagan, fr. pagus village); akin to OS. hēðin, adj., D. heiden a heathen, G. heide, OHG. heidan, Icel. heiðinn, adj., Sw. heden, Goth. haiþnō, n. fem. See Hea

senses.d: Gentile; pagan; as, a heathen author.
Barbarous; unenlightened; heathenish.
Irreligious; scoffing.
To cause to move upward or onward by a lifting effort; to lift; to raise; to hoist; — often with up; as, the wave heaved the boat on land.
q: One heaved ahigh, to be hurled down below.
Here a little child I stand, Heaving up my either hand.

senses.d: To throw; to cast; — obsolete, provincial, or colloquial, except in certain nautical phrases; as, to heave the lead; to heave the log.
To force from, or into, any position; to cause to move; also, to throw off; — mostly used in certain nautical phrases; as, to heave the ship ahead.
To raise or force from the breast; to utter with effort; as, to heave a sigh.
q: The wretched animal heaved forth such groans.

senses.d: To cause to swell or rise, as the breast or bosom.
q: The glittering, finny swarms That heave our friths, and crowd upon our shores.

Heave.etym: [OE. heven, hebben, AS. hebban; akin to OS. hebbian, D. heffen, OHG. heffan, hevan, G. heben, Icel. hefja, Sw. häfva, Dan. hæve, Goth. hafjan, L. capere to take, seize; cf. Gr. κώπη handle. Cf. Accept, Behoof, Capacious, Forceps, Haft, Receipt.]

senses.d: To be thrown up or raised; to rise upward, as a tower or mound.
q: And the huge columns heave into the sky.
Where heaves the turf in many a moldering heap.
The heaving sods of Bunker Hill.

senses.d: To rise and fall with alternate motions, as the lungs in heavy breathing, as waves in a heavy sea, as ships on the billows, as the earth when broken up by frost, etc.; to swell; to dilate; to expand; to distend; hence, to labor; to struggle.
q: Frequent for breath his panting bosom heaves.
The heaving plain of ocean.

senses.d: To make an effort to raise, throw, or move anything; to strain to do something difficult.
q: The Church of England had struggled and heaved at a reformation ever since Wyclif's days.

senses.d: To make an effort to vomit; to retch; to vomit.
An effort to raise something, as a weight, or one's self, or to move something heavy.
q: After many strains and heaves He got up to his saddle eaves.

senses.d: An upward motion; a rising; a swell or distention, as of the breast in difficult breathing, of the waves, of the earth in an earthquake, and the like.
q: There's matter in these sighs, these profound heaves, You must translate.
None could guess whether the next heave of the earthquake would settle . . . or swallow them.

senses.d: A horizontal dislocation in a metallic lode, taking place at an intersection with another lode.

The expanse of space surrounding the earth; esp., that which seems to be over the earth like a great arch or dome; the firmament; the sky; the place where the sun, moon, and stars appear; — often used in the plural in this sense.
q: I never saw the heavens so dim by day.
When my eyes shall be turned to behold for the last time the sun in heaven.

senses.d: The dwelling place of the Deity; the abode of bliss; the place or state of the blessed after death.
q: Unto the God of love, high heaven's King.
It is a knell That summons thee to heaven or to hell.
New thoughts of God, new hopes of Heaven.

senses.d: The sovereign of heaven; God; also, the assembly of the blessed, collectively; — used variously in this sense, as in No. 2.
q: Her prayers, whom Heaven delights to hear.
The will And high permission of all-ruling Heaven.

senses.d: Any place of supreme happiness or great comfort; perfect felicity; bliss; a sublime or exalted condition; as, a heaven of delight.
q: O bed! bed! delicious bed! That heaven upon earth to the weary head!

Heaven.etym: [OE. heven, hefen, heofen, AS. heofon; akin to OS. hevan, LG. heben, heven, Icel. hifinn; of uncertain origin, cf. D. hemel, G. himmel, Icel. himmin, Goth. himins; perh. akin to, or influenced by, the root of E. heave, or from a root signifying to cover, cf. Goth. gahamōn to put on, clothe one's sel

senses.d: To place in happiness or bliss, as if in heaven; to beatify.
q: We are happy as the bird whose nest Is heavened in the hush of purple hills.

senses.d: Pertaining to, resembling, or inhabiting heaven; celestial; not earthly; as, heavenly regions; heavenly music.
q: As is the heavenly, such are they also that are heavenly.

senses.d: Appropriate to heaven in character or happiness; perfect; pure; supremely blessed; as, a heavenly race; the heavenly, throng.
q: The love of heaven makes one heavenly.

senses.d: In a manner resembling that of heaven.
By the influence or agency of heaven.
q: Out heavenly guided soul shall climb.

senses.d: In a heavy manner; with great weight; as, to bear heavily on a thing; to be heavily loaded.
q: Heavily interested in those schemes of emigration.

senses.d: As if burdened with a great weight; slowly and laboriously; with difficulty; hence, in a slow, difficult, or suffering manner; sorrowfully.
q: And took off their chariot wheels, that they drave them heavily.
Why looks your grace so heavily to-day?

senses.d: The state or quality of being heavy in its various senses; weight; sadness; sluggishness; oppression; thickness.
Having the heaves.

Heaved or lifted with labor; not light; weighty; ponderous; as, a heavy stone; hence, sometimes, large in extent, quantity, or effects; as, a heavy fall of rain or snow; a heavy failure; heavy business transactions, etc.; often implying strength; as, a heavy barrier; also, difficult to move; as, a heavy draught.
Not easy to bear; burdensome; oppressive; hard to endure or accomplish; hence, grievous, afflictive; as, heavy yokes, expenses, undertakings, trials, news, etc.
q: The hand of the Lord was heavy upon them of Ashdod.
The king himself hath a heavy reckoning to make.
Sent hither to impart the heavy news.
Trust him not in matter of heavy consequence.

senses.d: Laden with that which is weighty; encumbered; burdened; bowed down, either with an actual burden, or with care, grief, pain, disappointment.
q: The heavy nobles all in council were.
A light wife doth make a heavy husband.

senses.d: Slow; sluggish; inactive; or lifeless, dull, inanimate, stupid; as, a heavy gait, looks, manners, style, and the like; a heavy writer or book.
q: Whilst the heavy plowman snores.
Of a heavy, dull, degenerate mind.
Neither his ear heavy, that it can not hear.

senses.d: Strong; violent; forcible; as, a heavy sea, storm, cannonade, and the like.
Loud; deep; — said of sound; as, heavy thunder.
q: But, hark! that heavy sound breaks in once more.

senses.d: Dark with clouds, or ready to rain; gloomy; — said of the sky.
Impeding motion; cloggy; clayey; — said of earth; as, a heavy road, soil, and the like.
Not raised or made light; as, heavy bread.
Not agreeable to, or suitable for, the stomach; not easily digested; — said of food.
Having much body or strength; — said of wines, or other liquors.
With child; pregnant.

Heavy.etym: [OE. hevi, AS. hefig, fr. hebban to lift, heave; akin to OHG. hebig, hevig, Icel. höfigr, höfugr. See Heave.]

senses.d: Heavily; — sometimes used in composition; as, heavy-laden.
To make heavy.
The goddess of youth, daughter of Jupiter and Juno. She was believed to have the power of restoring youth and beauty to those who had lost them.
An African ape; the hamadryas.

Hebe.etym: [L., fr. Gr. ἥβη youth, Ἥβη Hebe.]

senses.d: An appellative of Abraham or of one of his descendants, esp. in the line of Jacob; an Israelite; a Jew.
q: There came one that had escaped and told Abram the Hebrew.

senses.d: The language of the Hebrews; — one of the Semitic family of languages.

Hebrew.etym: [F. Hébreu, L. Hebraeus, Gr. �, fr. Heb. 'ibhrī.]

senses.d: Of or pertaining to the Hebrews; as, the Hebrew language or rites.
An Israelitish woman.

A thicket of bushes, usually thorn bushes; especially, such a thicket planted as a fence between any two portions of land; and also any sort of shrubbery, as evergreens, planted in a line or as a fence; particularly, such a thicket planted round a field to fence it, or in rows to separate the parts of a garden.
q: The roughest berry on the rudest hedge.
Through the verdant maze Of sweetbrier hedges I pursue my walk.

Hedge.etym: [OE. hegge, AS. hecg; akin to haga an inclosure, E. haw, AS. hege hedge, E. haybote, D. hegge, OHG. hegga, G. hecke. √12. See Haw a hedge.]

senses.d: To inclose or separate with a hedge; to fence with a thickly set line or thicket of shrubs or small trees; as, to hedge a field or garden.
To obstruct, as a road, with a barrier; to hinder from progress or success; — sometimes with up and out.
q: I will hedge up thy way with thorns.
Lollius Urbius . . . drew another wall . . . to hedge out incursions from the north.

senses.d: To surround for defense; to guard; to protect; to hem (in).
To surround so as to prevent escape.
q: That is a law to hedge in the cuckoo.

senses.d: To shelter one's self from danger, risk, duty, responsibility, etc., as if by hiding in or behind a hedge; to skulk; to slink; to shirk obligations.
q: I myself sometimes, leaving the fear of God on the left hand and hiding mine honor in my necessity, am fain to shuffle, to hedge and to lurch.

senses.d: To reduce the risk of a wager by making a bet against the side or chance one has bet on.
To use reservations and qualifications in one's speech so as to avoid committing one's self to anything definite.
q: The Heroic Stanzas read much more like an elaborate attempt to hedge between the parties than . . . to gain favor from the Roundheads.

senses.d: To mind; to regard with care; to take notice of; to attend to; to observe.
q: With pleasure Argus the musician heeds.

Heed.syn: To notice; regard; mind. See Attend, v. t.
Heed.etym: [OE. heden, AS. hēdan; akin to OS. hōdian, D. hoeden, Fries. hoda, OHG. huoten, G. hüten, Dan. hytte. √13. Cf. Hood.]

senses.d: To mind; to consider.
Attention; notice; observation; regard; — often with give or take.
q: With wanton heed and giddy cunning.
Amasa took no heed to the sword that was in Joab's hand.
Birds give more heed and mark words more than beasts.

senses.d: Careful consideration; obedient regard.
q: Therefore we ought to give the more earnest heed to the things which we have heard.

senses.d: A look or expression of heading.
q: He did it with a serious mind; a heed Was in his countenance.

senses.d: To lean or tip to one side, as a ship; as, the ship heels aport; the boat heeled over when the squall struck it.

Heel.etym: [OE. helden to lean, incline, AS. heldan, hyldan; akin to Icel. halla, Dan. helde, Sw. hälla to tilt, pour, and perh. to E. hill.]

senses.d: The hinder part of the foot; sometimes, the whole foot; — in man or quadrupeds.
q: He calls to mind his strength and then his speed, His winged heels and then his armed head.

senses.d: The hinder part of any covering for the foot, as of a shoe, sock, etc.; specif., a solid part projecting downward from the hinder part of the sole of a boot or shoe.
The latter or remaining part of anything; the closing or concluding part.
Anything regarded as like a human heel in shape; a protuberance; a knob.
The part of a thing corresponding in position to the human heel; the lower part, or part on which a thing rests
Management by the heel, especially the spurred heel; as, the horse understands the heel well.
The lower end of a timber in a frame, as a post or rafter. In the United States, specif., the obtuse angle of the lower end of a rafter set sloping.

Heel.etym: [OE. hele, heele, AS. hēla, perh. for hōhila, fr. AS. hōh heel (cf. Hough); but cf. D. hiel, OFries. heila, hēla, Icel. hæll, Dan. hæl, Sw. häl, and L. calx. √12. Cf. Inculcate.]

senses.d: To perform by the use of the heels, as in dancing, running, and the like.
q: I cannot sing, Nor heel the high lavolt.

senses.d: To add a heel to; as, to heel a shoe.
To arm with a gaff, as a cock for fighting.
The part of the face of the club head nearest the shaft.
In a carding machine, the part of a flat nearest the cylinder.
To hit (the ball) with the heel of the club.
To make (a fair catch) standing with one foot advanced, the heel on the ground and the toe up.
A young cow.

Heifer.etym: [OE. hayfare, AS. heáhfore, heáfore; the second part of this word seems akin to AS. fearr bull, ox; akin to OHG. farro, G. farre, D. vaars, heifer, G. färse, and perh. to Gr. �, �, calf, heifer.]

senses.d: The condition of being high; elevated position.
q: Behold the height of the stars, how high they are!

senses.d: The distance to which anything rises above its foot, above that on which in stands, above the earth, or above the level of the sea; altitude; the measure upward from a surface, as the floor or the ground, of an animal, especially of a man; stature.
q: height was six cubits and a span.

senses.d: Degree of latitude either north or south.
q: Guinea lieth to the north sea, in the same height as Peru to the south.

senses.d: That which is elevated; an eminence; a hill or mountain; as, Alpine heights.
Elevation in excellence of any kind, as in power, learning, arts; also, an advanced degree of social rank; preëminence or distinction in society; prominence.
q: Measure your mind's height by the shade it casts.
All would in his power hold, all make his subjects.

senses.d: Progress toward eminence; grade; degree.
q: Social duties are carried to greater heights, and enforced with stronger motives by the principles of our religion.
