senses.d: Utmost degree in extent; extreme limit of energy or condition; as, the height of a fever, of passion, of madness, of folly; the height of a tempest.
q: My grief was at the height before thou camest.

Height.etym: [OE. heighte, heght, heighthe, AS. heáhðu, hēhðu fr. heah high; akin to D. hoogte, Sw. höjd, Dan. höide, Icel. hæð, Goth. hauhiþa. See High.]

senses.d: Hateful; hatefully bad; flagrant; odious; atrocious; giving great offense; — applied to deeds or to character.
q: It were most heinous and accursed sacrilege.
How heinous had the fact been, how deserving Contempt!

Heinous.etym: [OF. haïnos hateful, F. haineux, fr. OF. haïne hate, F. haine, fr. haïr to hate; of German origin. See Hate.]

senses.d: One who inherits, or is entitled to succeed to the possession of, any property after the death of its owner; one on whom the law bestows the title or property of another at the death of the latter.
q: I am my father's heir and only son.

senses.d: One who receives any endowment from an ancestor or relation; as, the heir of one's reputation or virtues.
q: And I his heir in misery alone.

Heir.etym: [OE. heir, eir, hair, OF. heir, eir, F. hoir, L. heres; of uncertain origin. Cf. Hereditary, Heritage.]

senses.d: To inherit; to succeed to.
q: One only daughter heired the royal state.

senses.d: Health; welfare.
To hide; to cover; to roof.
q: Hide and hele things.

Hele.etym: [AS. helan, akin to D. helen, OHG. helan, G. hehlen, L. celare. √17. See Hell, and cf. Conceal.]

senses.d: The place of the dead, or of souls after death; the grave; — called in Hebrew sheol, and by the Greeks hades.
q: He descended into hell.
Thou wilt not leave my soul in hell.

senses.d: The place or state of punishment for the wicked after death; the abode of evil spirits. Hence, any mental torment; anguish.
q: It is a knell That summons thee to heaven or to hell.

senses.d: A place where outcast persons or things are gathered

Hell.etym: [AS. hell; akin to D. hel, OHG. hella, G. hölle, Icel. hal, Sw. helfvete, Dan. helvede, Goth. halja, and to AS. helan to conceal. ���. Cf. Hele, v. t., Conceal, Cell, Helmet, Hole, Occult.]

senses.d: To overwhelm.
The apparatus by which a ship is steered, comprising rudder, tiller, wheel, etc.; — commonly used of the tiller or wheel alone.
The place or office of direction or administration.
One at the place of direction or control; a steersman; hence, a guide; a director.
q: The helms o' the State, who care for you like fathers.

senses.d: A helve.

Helm.etym: [OE. helme, AS. helma rudder; akin to D. & G. helm, Icel. hjālm, and perh. to E. helve.]

senses.d: To steer; to guide; to direct.
q: The business he hath helmed.
A wild wave . . . overbears the bark, And him that helms it.

senses.d: A helmet.
A heavy cloud lying on the brow of a mountain.
To cover or furnish with a helm or helmet.
q: She that helmed was in starke stours.

senses.d: A defensive covering for the head. See Casque, Headpiece, Morion, Sallet, and Illust. of Beaver.
The representation of a helmet over shields or coats of arms, denoting gradations of rank by modifications of form.

A helmet-shaped hat, made of cork, felt, metal, or other suitable material, worn as part of the uniform of soldiers, firemen, etc., also worn in hot countries as a protection from the heat of the sun.
That which resembles a helmet in form, position, etc.

Helmet.etym: [OF. helmet, a dim of helme, F. heaume; of Teutonic origin; cf. G. helm, akin to AS. & OS. helm, D. helm, helmet, Icel. hjālmr, Sw. hjelm, Dan. hielm, Goth. hilms; and prob. from the root of AS. helan to hide, to hele; cf. also Lith. szalmas, Russ. shleme, Skr. çarman protection. √17. Cf. Hele, Hell

senses.d: To furnish with strength or means for the successful performance of any action or the attainment of any object; to aid; to assist; as, to help a man in his work; to help one to remember; — the following infinitive is commonly used without to; as, “Help me scale yon balcony.”
To furnish with the means of deliverance from trouble; as, to help one in distress; to help one out of prison.
To furnish with relief, as in pain or disease; to be of avail against; — sometimes with of before a word designating the pain or disease, and sometimes having such a word for the direct object.
q: The true calamus helps coughs.

senses.d: To change for the better; to remedy.
q: Cease to lament for what thou canst not help.

senses.d: To prevent; to hinder; as, the evil approaches, and who can help it?
To forbear; to avoid.
q: I can not help remarking the resemblance betwixt him and our author.

senses.d: To wait upon, as the guests at table, by carving and passing food.

Help.syn: To aid; assist; succor; relieve; serve; support; sustain; befriend.
Help.etym: [AS. helpan; akin to OS. helpan, D. helpen, G. helfen, OHG. helfan, Icel. hjālpa, Sw. hjelpa, Dan. hielpe, Goth. hilpan; cf. Lith. szelpti, and Skr. klp to be fitting.]

senses.d: To lend aid or assistance; to contribute strength or means; to avail or be of use; to assist.
q: A generous present helps to persuade, as well as an agreeable person.

senses.d: Strength or means furnished toward promoting an object, or deliverance from difficulty or distress; aid; ^; also, the person or thing furnishing the aid; as, he gave me a help of fifty dollars.
q: Give us help from trouble, for vain is the help of man.
God is . . . a very present help in trouble.
Virtue is a friend and a help to nature.

senses.d: Remedy; relief; as, there is no help for it.
A helper; one hired to help another; also, thew hole force of hired helpers in any business.
Specifically, a domestic servant, man or woman.

Help.etym: [AS. help; akin to D. hulp, G. hülfe, hilfe, Icel. hjālp, Sw. hjelp, Dan. hielp. See Help, v. t.]

senses.d: One who, or that which, helps, aids, assists, or relieves; as, a lay helper in a parish.
q: Thou art the helper of the fatherless.
Compassion . . . oftentimes a helper of evils.

senses.d: The handle of an ax, hatchet, or adze.
The lever at the end of which is the hammer head, in a forge hammer.

Helve.etym: [OE. helve, helfe, AS. hielf, helf, hylf, cf. OHG. halb; and also E. halter, helm of a rudder.]

senses.d: To furnish with a helve, as an ax.
Them

Hem.etym: [OE., fr. AS. him, heom, dative pl. of. hē he. See He, They.]

senses.d: An onomatopoetic word used as an expression of hesitation, doubt, etc. It is often a sort of voluntary half cough, loud or subdued, and would perhaps be better expressed by hm.
q: Cough or cry hem, if anybody come.

senses.d: An utterance or sound of the voice, hem or hm, often indicative of hesitation or doubt, sometimes used to call attention.
To make the sound expressed by the word hem; hence, to hesitate in speaking.
The edge or border of a garment or cloth, doubled over and sewed, to strengthen it and prevent raveling.
Border; edge; margin.
A border made on sheet-metal ware by doubling over the edge of the sheet, to stiffen it and remove the sharp edge.

Hem.etym: [AS. hem, border, margin; cf. Fries. hämel, Prov. G. hammel hem of mire or dirt.]

senses.d: To form a hem or border to; to fold and sew down the edge of.
To border; to edge
q: All the skirt about Was hemmed with golden fringe.

senses.d: The name of several poisonous umbelliferous herbs having finely cut leaves and small white flowers, as the Cicuta maculata, bulbifera, and virosa, and the Conium maculatum. See Conium.
An evergreen tree common in North America (Abies, or Tsuga, Canadensis); hemlock spruce.
q: The murmuring pines and the hemlocks.

senses.d: The wood or timber of the hemlock tree.
The female of the domestic fowl; also, the female of grouse, pheasants, or any kind of birds; as, the heath hen; the gray hen.

Hen.etym: [AS. henn, hen, hæn; akin to D. hen, OHG. henna, G. henne, Icel. h�na, Dan. höna; the fem. corresponding to AS. hana cock, D. haan, OHG. hano, G. hahn, Icel. hani, Dan. & Sw. hane. Prob. akin to L. canere to sing, and orig. meaning, a singer. Cf. Chanticleer.]

senses.d: From this place; away.
q: Arise, let us go hence.
I will send thee far hence unto the Gentiles.

senses.d: From this time; in the future; as, a week hence.
From this reason; as an inference or deduction.
q: Hence, perhaps, it is, that Solomon calls the fear of the Lord the beginning of wisdom.

senses.d: From this source or origin.
q: All other faces borrowed hence Their light and grace.
Whence come wars and fightings among you? Come they not hence, even of your lusts?
An ancient author prophesied from hence.
Expelled from hence into a world Of woe and sorrow.

Hence.etym: [OE. hennes, hens (the s is prop. a genitive ending; cf. -wards), also hen, henne, hennen, heonnen, heonene, AS. heonan, heonon, heona, hine; akin to OHG. hinnān, G. hinnen, OHG. hina, G. hin; all from the root of E. he. See He.]

senses.d: To send away.
From this time forward; henceforward.
q: I never from thy side henceforth to stray.

senses.d: From this time forward; henceforth.
The form of the objective and the possessive case of the personal pronoun she; as, I saw her with her purse out.

Her.etym: [OE. hire, here, hir, hure, gen. and dat. sing., AS. hire, gen. and dat. sing. of héo she. from the same root as E. he. See He.]

senses.d: Of them; their.
q: On here bare knees adown they fall.

Her.etym: [OE. here, hire, AS. heora, hyra, gen. pl. of hē. See He.]

senses.d: An officer whose business was to denounce or proclaim war, to challenge to battle, to proclaim peace, and to bear messages from the commander of an army. He was invested with a sacred and inviolable character.

In the Middle Ages, the officer charged with the above duties, and also with the care of genealogies, of the rights and privileges of noble families, and especially of armorial bearings. In modern times, some vestiges of this office remain, especially in England. See Heralds' College (below), and King-at-Arms.
A proclaimer; one who, or that which, publishes or announces; as, the herald of another's fame.
A forerunner; a a precursor; a harbinger.
q: It was the lark, the herald of the morn.

senses.d: Any messenger.

Herald.etym: [OE. herald, heraud, OF. heralt, heraut, herault, F. héraut, LL. heraldus, haraldus, fr. (assumed) OHG. heriwalto, hariwaldo, a (civil) officer who serves the army; hari, heri, army + waltan to manage, govern, G. walten; akin to E. wield. See Harry, Wield.]

senses.d: To introduce, or give tidings of, as by a herald; to proclaim; to announce; to foretell; to usher in.
A plant whose stem does not become woody and permanent, but dies, at least down to the ground, after flowering.
Grass; herbage.
q: And flocks Grazing the tender herb.

Herb.etym: [OE. herbe, erbe, OF. herbe, erbe, F. herbe, L. herba; perh. akin to Gr. φορβή food, pasture, φέρβειν to feed.]

senses.d: Haired.
A number of beasts assembled together; as, a herd of horses, oxen, cattle, camels, elephants, deer, or swine; a particular stock or family of cattle.
q: The lowing herd wind slowly o'er the lea.

senses.d: A crowd of low people; a rabble.
q: But far more numerous was the herd of such Who think too little and who talk too much.
You can never interest the common herd in the abstract question.

Herd.etym: [OE. herd, heord, AS. heord; akin to OHG. herta,G. herde, Icel. hjör�, Sw. hjord, Dan. hiord, Goth. haírda; cf. Skr. çardha troop, host.]

senses.d: One who herds or assembles domestic animals; a herdsman; — much used in composition; as, a shepherd; a goatherd, and the like.

Herd.etym: [OE. hirde, herde, heorde, AS. hirde, hyrde, heorde; akin to G. hirt, hirte, OHG. hirti, Icel. hir�ir, Sw. herde, Dan. hyrde, Goth. haírdeis. See 2d Herd.]

senses.d: To unite or associate in a herd; to feed or run together, or in company; as, sheep herd on many hills.
To associate; to ally one's self with, or place one's self among, a group or company.
q: I'll herd among his friends, and seem One of the number.

senses.d: To act as a herdsman or a shepherd.
To form or put into a herd.
The owner or keeper of a herd or of herds; one employed in tending a herd of cattle.
Hair.
Her; hers. See Her.
In this place; in the place where the speaker is; — opposed to there.
q: He is not here, for he is risen.

senses.d: In the present life or state.
q: Happy here, and more happy hereafter.

senses.d: To or into this place; hither. See Thither.
q: Here comes Virgil.
Thou led'st me here.

senses.d: At this point of time, or of an argument; now.
q: The prisoner here made violent efforts to rise.

Here.etym: [OE. her, AS. h�r; akin to OS. h�r, D. hier, OHG. hiar, G. hier, Icel. & Goth. h�r, Dan. her, Sw. här; fr. root of E. he. See He.]

senses.d: In time to come; in some future time or state.
q: Hereafter he from war shall come.

senses.d: A future existence or state.
q: 'Tis Heaven itself that points out an hereafter.

senses.d: By means of this.
q: And hereby we do know that we know him.

senses.d: Close by; very near.
In this.
q: Herein is my Father glorified, that ye bear much fruit.

senses.d: Of this; concerning this; from this; hence.
q: Hereof comes it that Prince Harry is valiant.

senses.d: An opinion held in opposition to the established or commonly received doctrine, and tending to promote a division or party, as in politics, literature, philosophy, etc.; — usually, but not necessarily, said in reproach.
q: New opinions Divers and dangerous, which are heresies, And, not reformed, may prove pernicious.

After the study of philosophy began in Greece, and the philosophers, disagreeing amongst themselves, had started many questions . . . because every man took what opinion he pleased, each several opinion was called a heresy; which signified no more than a private opinion, without reference to truth or falsehood.

senses.d: Religious opinion opposed to the authorized doctrinal standards of any particular church, especially when tending to promote schism or separation; lack of orthodox or sound belief; rejection of, or erroneous belief in regard to, some fundamental religious doctrine or truth; heterodoxy.
q: Doubts 'mongst divines, and difference of texts, From whence arise diversity of sects, And hateful heresies by God abhor'd.
Deluded people! that do not consider that the greatest heresy in the world is a wicked life.

senses.d: An offense against Christianity, consisting in a denial of some essential doctrine, which denial is publicly avowed, and obstinately maintained.
q: A second offense is that of heresy, which consists not in a total denial of Christianity, but of some its essential doctrines, publicly and obstinately avowed.

Heresy.etym: [OE. heresie, eresie, OF. heresie, iresie, F. hérésie, L. haeresis, Gr. � a taking, a taking for one's self, choosing, a choice, a sect, a heresy, fr. � to take, choose.]

senses.d: Up to this time; hitherto; before; in time past.
Unto this; up to this time; hereto.
With this.
That which is inherited, or passes from heir to heir; inheritance.
q: Part of my heritage, Which my dead father did bequeath to me.

senses.d: A possession; the Israelites, as God's chosen people; also, a flock under pastoral charge.

Heritage.etym: [OE. heritage, eritage, OF. heritage, eritage, F. héritage, fr. hériter to inherit, LL. heriditare. See Hereditable.]

senses.d: Originally, a boundary stone dedicated to Hermes as the god of boundaries, and therefore bearing in some cases a head, or head and shoulders, placed upon a quadrangular pillar whose height is that of the body belonging to the head, sometimes having feet or other parts of the body sculptured upon it. These figures, though often representing Hermes, were used for other divinities, and even, in later times, for portraits of human beings. Called also herma. See Terminal statue, under Terminal.
One of a party among the Jews, composed of partisans of Herod of Galilee. They joined with the Pharisees against Christ.

Any wading bird of the genus Ardea and allied genera, of the family Ardeidæ. The herons have a long, sharp bill, and long legs and toes, with the claw of the middle toe toothed. The common European heron (Ardea cinerea) is remarkable for its directly ascending flight, and was formerly hunted with the larger falcons.

Heron.etym: [OE. heiroun, heroun, heron, hern, OF. hairon, F. héron, OHG. heigir; cf. Icel. hegri, Dan. heire, Sw. häger, and also G. häher jay, jackdaw, OHG. hehara, higere, woodpecker, magpie, D. reiger heron, G. reiher, AS. hrāgra. Cf. Aigret, Egret.]

senses.d: An emphasized form of the third person feminine pronoun; — used as a subject with she; as, she herself will bear the blame; also used alone in the predicate, either in the nominative or objective case; as, it is herself; she blames herself.
Her own proper, true, or real character; hence, her right, or sane, mind; as, the woman was deranged, but she is now herself again; she has come to herself.
To cut with an ax; to fell with a sharp instrument; — often with down, or off.
To form or shape with a sharp instrument; to cut; hence, to form laboriously; — often with out; as, to hew out a sepulcher.
q: Look unto the rock whence ye are hewn.
Rather polishing old works than hewing out new.

senses.d: To cut in pieces; to chop; to hack.
q: Hew them to pieces; hack their bones asunder.

Hew.etym: [AS. heáwan; akin to D. houwen, OHG. houwan, G. hauen, Icel. höggva, Sw. hugga, Dan. hugge, Lith. kova battle, Russ. kovate to hammer, forge. Cf. Hay cut grass, Hoe.]

senses.d: Destruction by cutting down.
q: Of whom he makes such havoc and such hew.

senses.d: Hue; color.
Shape; form.
A domestic servant; a retainer.
One who hews.
Felled, cut, or shaped as with an ax; roughly squared; as, a house built of hewn logs.
Roughly dressed as with a hammer; as, hewn stone.
from Hide. Concealed; put out of view; secret; not known; mysterious.
q: Bring to light the hidden things of darkness.
My heart, which by a secret harmony Still moves with thine, joined in connection sweet.
By what best way, Whether of open war, or covert guile, We now debate.

senses.d: To conceal, or withdraw from sight; to put out of view; to secrete.
q: A city that is set on an hill can not be hid.
If circumstances lead me, I will find Where truth is hid.

senses.d: To withhold from knowledge; to keep secret; to refrain from avowing or confessing.
q: Heaven from all creatures hides the book of fate.

senses.d: To remove from danger; to shelter.
q: In the time of trouble he shall hide me in his pavilion.

Hide.syn: To conceal; secrete; disguise; dissemble; screen; cloak; mask; veil. See Conceal.
Hide.etym: [OE. hiden, huden, AS. hȳdan; akin to Gr. κεύθειν, and prob. to E. house, hut, and perh. to E. hide of an animal, and to hoard. Cf. Hoard.]

senses.d: To lie concealed; to keep one's self out of view; to be withdrawn from sight or observation.
q: Bred to disguise, in public 'tis you hide.

senses.d: An abode or dwelling.
A measure of land, common in Domesday Book and old English charters, the quantity of which is not well ascertained, but has been differently estimated at 80, 100, and 120 acres.

Hide.etym: [AS. hīd, earlier hīged; prob. orig., land enough to support a family; cf. AS. hīwan, hīgan, members of a household, and E. hind a peasant.]

senses.d: The skin of an animal, either raw or dressed; — generally applied to the undressed skins of the larger domestic animals, as oxen, horses, etc.
The human skin; — so called in contempt.
q: O tiger's heart, wrapped in a woman's hide!

Hide.etym: [OE. hide, hude, AS. hȳd; akin to D. huid, OHG. hūt, G. haut, Icel. hūð, Dan. & Sw. hud, L. cutis, Gr. κύτοσ; and cf. Gr. σκύτοσ skin, hide, L. scutum shield, and E. sky. √13.]

senses.d: To flog; to whip.
The act of hiding or concealing, or of withholding from view or knowledge; concealment.
q: There was the hiding of his power.

senses.d: A flogging.
To hie.
q: Men must high them apace, and make haste.

senses.d: Elevated above any starting point of measurement, as a line, or surface; having altitude; lifted up; raised or extended in the direction of the zenith; lofty; tall; as, a high mountain, tower, tree; the sun is high.
Regarded as raised up or elevated; distinguished; remarkable; conspicuous; superior; — used indefinitely or relatively, and often in figurative senses, which are understood from the connection
Elevated in character or quality, whether moral or intellectual; preëminent; honorable; as, high aims, or motives.
Exalted in social standing or general estimation, or in rank, reputation, office, and the like; dignified; as, she was welcomed in the highest circles.
q: He was a wight of high renown.

senses.d: Of noble birth; illustrious; as, of high family.
Of great strength, force, importance, and the like; strong; mighty; powerful; violent; sometimes, triumphant; victorious; majestic, etc.; as, a high wind; high passions.
q: Strong is thy hand, and high is thy right hand.
Can heavenly minds such high resentment show?

senses.d: Very abstract; difficult to comprehend or surmount; grand; noble.
q: Both meet to hear and answer such high things.
Plain living and high thinking are no more.

senses.d: Costly; dear in price; extravagant; as, to hold goods at a high price.
q: If they must be good at so high a rate, they know they may be safe at a cheaper.

senses.d: Arrogant; lofty; boastful; proud; ostentatious; — used in a bad sense.
q: An high look and a proud heart . . . is sin.
His forces, after all the high discourses, amounted really but to eighteen hundred foot.

senses.d: Possessing a characteristic quality in a supreme or superior degree; as, high (i. e., intense) heat; high (i.e., full or quite) noon; high (i.e., rich or spicy) seasoning; high (i.e., complete) pleasure; high (i.e., deep or vivid) color; high (i.e., extensive, thorough) scholarship, etc.
q: High time it is this war now ended were.
High sauces and spices are fetched from the Indies.

senses.d: Strong-scented; slightly tainted; as, epicures do not cook game before it is high.
Acute or sharp; — opposed to grave or low; as, a high note.

High.syn: Tall; lofty; elevated; noble; exalted; supercilious; proud; violent; full; dear. See Tall.
High.etym: [OE. high, hegh, hey, heh, AS. heáh, h�h; akin to OS. h�h, OFries. hag, hach, D. hoog, OHG. h�h, G. hoch, Icel. h�r, Sw. hög, Dan. höi, Goth. hauhs, and to Icel. haugr mound, G. hügel hill, Lith. kaukaras.]

senses.d: In a high manner; in a high place; to a great altitude; to a great degree; largely; in a superior manner; eminently; powerfully.
An elevated place; a superior region; a height; the sky; heaven.
People of rank or high station; as, high and low.
The highest card dealt or drawn.
To rise; as, the sun higheth.
In a high manner, or to a high degree; very much; as, highly esteemed.
The state of being high; elevation; loftiness.
A title of honor given to kings, princes, or other persons of rank; as, His Royal Highness.
A road or way open to the use of the public; a main road or thoroughfare.
A natural elevation of land, or a mass of earth rising above the common level of the surrounding land; an eminence less than a mountain.
q: Every mountain and hill shall be made low.

senses.d: The earth raised about the roots of a plant or cluster of plants. See Hill, v. t.
A single cluster or group of plants growing close together, and having the earth heaped up about them; as, a hill of corn or potatoes.

Hill.etym: [OE. hil, hul, AS. hyll; akin to OD. hille, hil, L. collis, and prob. to E. haulm, holm, and column. Cf. 2d Holm.]

senses.d: To surround with earth; to heap or draw earth around or upon; as, to hill corn.
q: Showing them how to plant and hill it.

senses.d: Them. See Hem.
The objective case of he. See He.
q: Him that is weak in the faith receive.
Friends who have given him the most sympathy.
I never saw but Humphrey, duke of Gloster, Did bear him like a noble gentleman.

Him.etym: [AS. him, dat. of hē. √183. See He.]

senses.d: An emphasized form of the third person masculine pronoun; — used as a subject usually with he; as, he himself will bear the blame; used alone in the predicate, either in the nominative or objective case; as, it is himself who saved himself.
q: But he himself returned from the quarries.
David hid himself in the field.
The Lord himself shall give you a sign.
Who gave himself for us, that he might . . . purify unto himself a peculiar people.
With shame remembers, while himself was one Of the same herd, himself the same had done.
It comprehendeth in himself all good.

senses.d: One's true or real character; one's natural temper and disposition; the state of being in one's right or sane mind (after unconsciousness, passion, delirium, or abasement); as, the man has come to himself.
Themselves. See Hemself.
A Hebrew measure of liquids, containing three quarts, one pint, one gill, English measure.
The female of the red deer, of which the male is the stag.
A spotted food fish of the genus Epinephelus, as E. apua of Bermuda, and E. Drummond-hayi of Florida; — called also coney, John Paw, spotted hind.

Hind.etym: [AS. hind; akin to D. hinde, OHG. hinta, G. hinde, hindin, Icel., Sw., & Dan. hind, and perh. to Goth. hinpan to seize (in comp.), E. hunt, or cf. Gr. � a young deer.]

senses.d: A domestic; a servant.
A peasant; a rustic; a farm servant.
q: The hind, that homeward driving the slow steer Tells how man's daily work goes forward here.

Hind.etym: [OE. hine, AS. hīne, hīna, orig. gen. pl. of hīwan domestics; akin to Icel. hjū man and wife, domestics, family, Goth. heiwafrauja master of the house, G. heirath marriage; cf. L. civis citizen, E. city or E. home. Cf. Hide a measure of land.]

senses.d: In the rear; — opposed to front; of or pertaining to the part or end which follows or is behind, in opposition to the part which leads or is before; as, the hind legs or hind feet of a quadruped; the hind man in a procession.

Hind.etym: [OE. hind, adv., back, AS. hindan behind. See Hinder, a.]

senses.d: Of or belonging to that part or end which is in the rear, or which follows; as, the hinder part of a wagon; the hinder parts of a horse.
q: He was in the hinder part of the ship.

Hinder.etym: [OE. hindere, AS. hinder, adv., behind; akin to OHG. hintar, prep., behind, G. hinter, Goth. hindar; orig. a comparative, and akin to AS. hine hence. See Hence, He, and cf. Hind, a., Hindmost.]

senses.d: To keep back or behind; to prevent from starting or moving forward; to check; to retard; to obstruct; to bring to a full stop; — often followed by from; as, an accident hindered the coach; drought hinders the growth of plants; to hinder me from going.
q: Them that were entering in ye hindered.
I hinder you too long.

senses.d: To prevent or embarrass; to debar; to shut out.
q: What hinders younger brothers, being fathers of families, from having the same right?

Hinder.syn: To check; retard; impede; delay; block; clog; prevent; stop; interrupt; counteract; thwart; oppose; obstruct; debar; embarrass.
Hinder.etym: [OE. hindren, hinderen, AS. hindrian, fr. hinder behind; akin to D. hinderen, G. hindern, OHG. hintar�n, Icel. & Sw. hindra, Dan. hindre. See Hinder, a.]

senses.d: To interpose obstacles or impediments; to be a hindrance.
q: This objection hinders not but that the heroic action of some commander . . . may be written.

senses.d: Furthest in or toward the rear; last.

Hindermost.etym: [The superlative of hind. See Hind, a.]

senses.d: The hook with its eye, or the joint, on which a door, gate, lid, etc., turns or swings; a flexible piece, as a strip of leather, which serves as a joint to turn on.
q: The gate self-opened wide, On golden hinges turning.

senses.d: That on which anything turns or depends; a governing principle; a cardinal point or rule; as, this argument was the hinge on which the question turned.
One of the four cardinal points, east, west, north, or south.
q: When the moon is in the hinge at East.
Nor slept the winds . . . but rushed abroad.

Hinge.etym: [OE. henge, heeng; akin to D. heng, LG. henge, Prov. E. hingle a small hinge; connected with hang, v., and Icel. hengja to hang. See Hang.]

senses.d: To attach by, or furnish with, hinges.
To bend.
To stand, depend, hang, or turn, as on a hinge; to depend chiefly for a result or decision or for force and validity; — usually with on or upon; as, the argument hinges on this point.
The projecting region of the lateral parts of one side of the pelvis and the hip joint; the haunch; the huckle.
The external angle formed by the meeting of two sloping sides or skirts of a roof, which have their wall plates running in different directions.
In a bridge truss, the place where an inclined end post meets the top chord.

Hip.etym: [OE. hipe, huppe, AS. hype; akin to D. heup, OHG. huf, G. hüfte, Dan. hofte, Sw. höft, Goth. hups; cf. Icel. huppr, and also Gr. � the hollow above the hips of cattle, and Lith. kumpis ham.]

senses.d: To dislocate or sprain the hip of, to fracture or injure the hip bone of (a quadruped) in such a manner as to produce a permanent depression of that side.
To throw (one's adversary) over one's hip in wrestling (technically called cross buttock).
To make with a hip or hips, as a roof.
The fruit of a rosebush, especially of the English dog-rose (Rosa canina).

Hip.etym: [OE. hepe, AS. heópe; cf. OHG. hiufo a bramble bush.]

senses.d: Used to excite attention or as a signal; as, hip, hip, hurra!
The price, reward, or compensation paid, or contracted to be paid, for the temporary use of a thing or a place, for personal service, or for labor; wages; rent; pay.
q: The laborer is worthy of his hire.

senses.d: A bailment by which the use of a thing, or the services and labor of a person, are contracted for at a certain price or reward.

Hire.etym: [OE. hire, hure, AS. hȳr; akin to D. huur, G. heuer, Dan. hyre, Sw. hyra.]

senses.d: To procure (any chattel or estate) from another person, for temporary use, for a compensation or equivalent; to purchase the use or enjoyment of for a limited time; as, to hire a farm for a year; to hire money.
To engage or purchase the service, labor, or interest of (any one) for a specific purpose, by payment of wages; as, to hire a servant, an agent, or an advocate.

To grant the temporary use of, for compensation; to engage to give the service of, for a price; to let; to lease; — now usually with out, and often reflexively; as, he has hired out his horse, or his time.
q: They . . . have hired out themselves for bread.

Hire.etym: [OE. hiren, huren, AS. hȳrian; akin to D. huren, G. heuern, Dan. hyre, Sw. hyra. See Hire, n.]

senses.d: One who is hired, or who serves for wages; esp., one whose motive and interest in serving another are wholly gainful; a mercenary.
Serving for hire or wages; venal; mercenary.
Hers; theirs. See Here, pron.
Belonging or pertaining to him; — used as a pronominal adjective or adjective pronoun; as, tell John his papers are ready; formerly used also for its, but this use is now obsolete.
q: No comfortable star did lend his light.
Who can impress the forest, bid the tree Unfix his earth-bound root?

senses.d: The possessive of he; as, the book is his.

His.etym: [AS. his of him, his, gen. masc. & neut. of h�, neut. hit. See He.]

senses.d: To make with the mouth a prolonged sound like that of the letter s, by driving the breath between the tongue and the teeth; to make with the mouth a sound like that made by a goose or a snake when angered; esp., to make such a sound as an expression of hatred, passion, or disapproval.
q: The merchants among the people shall hiss at thee.

senses.d: To make a similar noise by any means; to pass with a sibilant sound; as, the arrow hissed as it flew.
q: Shod with steel, We hissed along the polished ice.

Hiss.etym: [AS. hysian; prob. of imitative origin�; cf. LG. hissen, OD. hisschen.]

senses.d: To condemn or express contempt for by hissing.
q: If the tag-rag people did not clap him and hiss him, according as he pleased and displeased them.
Malcolm. What is the newest grief? Ros. That of an hour's age doth hiss the speaker.

senses.d: To utter with a hissing sound.
q: The long-necked geese of the world that are ever hissing dispraise.

senses.d: A prolonged sound like that letter s, made by forcing out the breath between the tongue and teeth, esp. as a token of disapprobation or contempt.
q: “Hiss” implies audible friction of breath consonants.
A dismal, universal hiss, the sound Of public scorn.

senses.d: Any sound resembling that above described
q: But hiss for hiss returned with forked tongue.

senses.d: The note of a goose when irritated.
The noise made by steam escaping through a narrow orifice, or by water falling on a hot stove.
The act of emitting a hiss or hisses.
The occasion of contempt; the object of scorn and derision.
q: I will make this city desolate, and a hissing.

senses.d: It.
To reach with a stroke or blow; to strike or touch, usually with force; especially, to reach or touch (an object aimed at).
q: I think you have hit the mark.

senses.d: To reach or attain exactly; to meet according to the occasion; to perform successfully; to attain to; to accord with; to be conformable to; to suit.
q: Birds learning tunes, and their endeavors to hit the notes right.
There you hit him; . . . that argument never fails with him.
Whose saintly visage is too bright To hit the sense of human sight.
He scarcely hit my humor.

senses.d: To guess; to light upon or discover.
To take up, or replace by a piece belonging to the opposing player; — said of a single unprotected piece on a point.

Hit.etym: [OE. hitten, hutten, of Scand. origin; cf. Dan. hitte to hit, find, Sw. & Icel. hitta.]

senses.d: To meet or come in contact; to strike; to clash; — followed by against or on.
q: If bodies be extension alone, how can they move and hit one against another?
Corpuscles, meeting with or hitting on those bodies, become conjoined with them.

senses.d: To meet or reach what was aimed at or desired; to succeed, — often with implied chance, or luck.
q: And oft it hits Where hope is coldest and despair most fits.
And millions miss for one that hits.

senses.d: A striking against; the collision of one body against another; the stroke that touches anything.
q: So he the famed Cilician fencer praised, And, at each hit, with wonder seems amazed.

senses.d: A stroke of success in an enterprise, as by a fortunate chance; as, he made a hit.
q: What late he called a blessing, now was wit, And God's good providence, a lucky hit.

senses.d: A peculiarly apt expression or turn of thought; a phrase which hits the mark; as, a happy hit.
A game won at backgammon after the adversary has removed some of his men. It counts less than a gammon.
A striking of the ball; as, a safe hit; a foul hit; — sometimes used specifically for a base hit.
A port or small haven; — used in composition; as, Lambhithe, now Lambeth.
To this place; — used with verbs signifying motion, and implying motion toward the speaker; correlate of hence and thither; as, to come or bring hither.
To this point, source, conclusion, design, etc.; — in a sense not physical.
q: Hither we refer whatsoever belongeth unto the highest perfection of man.

Hither.etym: [OE. hider, AS. hider; akin to Icel. hēðra, Dan. hid, Sw. hit, Goth. hidrē; cf. L. citra on this side, or E. here, he. √183. Cf. He.]

senses.d: Being on the side next or toward the person speaking; nearer; — correlate of thither and farther; as, on the hither side of a hill.
Applied to time: On the hither side of, younger than; of fewer years than.
q: And on the hither side, or so she looked, Of twenty summers.
To the present generation, that is to say, the people a few years on the hither and thither side of thirty, the name of Charles Darwin stands alongside of those of Isaac Newton and Michael Faraday.

senses.d: To this place; to a prescribed limit.
q: Hitherto shalt thou come, but no further.

senses.d: Up to this time; as yet; until now.
q: The Lord hath blessed me hitherto.

senses.d: Who.
A stop; a halt; a moderation of pace.
q: There is no ho with them.

senses.d: Halloo! attend! — a call to excite attention, or to give notice of approach.
Stop! stand still! hold! — a word now used by teamsters, but formerly to order the cessation of anything.
q: The duke . . . pulled out his sword and cried “Hoo!”
An herald on a scaffold made an hoo.

senses.d: White, or grayish white; as, hoar frost; hoar cliffs.
Gray or white with age; hoary.
q: Whose beard with age is hoar.
Old trees with trunks all hoar.

senses.d: Musty; moldy; stale.

Hoar.etym: [OE. hor, har, AS. hār; akin to Icel. hārr, and to OHG. hēr illustrious, magnificent; cf. Icel. Heið brightness of the sky, Goth. hais torch, Skr. kētus light, torch. Cf. Hoary.]

senses.d: Hoariness; antiquity.
q: Covered with the awful hoar of innumerable ages.

senses.d: To become moldy or musty.
The white particles formed by the congelation of dew; white frost.
q: He scattereth the hoarfrost like ashes.

senses.d: White or whitish.
White or gray with age; hoar; as, hoary hairs.
q: Reverence the hoary head.

senses.d: remote in time past; as, hoary antiquity.
Moldy; mossy; musty.
Of a pale silvery gray.
Covered with short, dense, grayish white hairs; canescent.
A kind of wooden tray with a handle, borne on the shoulder, for carrying mortar, brick, etc.
A utensil for holding coal; a coal scuttle.

Hod.etym: [Prov. E. for hold, i. e., that which holds. See Hold.]

senses.d: To hoist.
q: They . . . hoised up the mainsail to the wind.

senses.d: Whole.
The whole interior portion of a vessel below the lower deck, in which the cargo is stowed.
To cause to remain in a given situation, position, or relation, within certain limits, or the like; to prevent from falling or escaping; to sustain; to restrain; to keep in the grasp; to retain.
q: The loops held one curtain to another.
Thy right hand shall hold me.
They all hold swords, being expert in war.
In vain he seeks, that having can not hold.
France, thou mayst hold a serpent by the tongue, . . . A fasting tiger safer by the tooth, Than keep in peace that hand which thou dost hold.

senses.d: To retain in one's keeping; to maintain possession of, or authority over; not to give up or relinquish; to keep; to defend.
q: We mean to hold what anciently we claim Of deity or empire.

senses.d: To have; to possess; to be in possession of; to occupy; to derive title to; as, to hold office.
q: This noble merchant held a noble house.
Of him to hold his seigniory for a yearly tribute.
And now the strand, and now the plain, they held.

senses.d: To impose restraint upon; to limit in motion or action; to bind legally or morally; to confine; to restrain.
q: We can not hold mortality's strong hand.
Death! what do'st? O, hold thy blow.
He had not sufficient judgment and self-command to hold his tongue.

senses.d: To maintain in being or action; to carry on; to prosecute, as a course of conduct or an argument; to continue; to sustain.
q: Hold not thy peace, and be not still.
Seedtime and harvest, heat and hoary frost, Shall hold their course.

senses.d: To prosecute, have, take, or join in, as something which is the result of united action; as to, hold a meeting, a festival, a session, etc.; hence, to direct and bring about officially; to conduct or preside at; as, the general held a council of war; a judge holds a court; a clergyman holds a service.
q: I would hold more talk with thee.

senses.d: To receive and retain; to contain as a vessel; as, this pail holds milk; hence, to be able to receive and retain; to have capacity or containing power for.
q: Broken cisterns that can hold no water.
One sees more devils than vast hell can hold.

senses.d: To accept, as an opinion; to be the adherent of, openly or privately; to persist in, as a purpose; to maintain; to sustain.
q: Stand fast and hold the traditions which ye have been taught.
But still he held his purpose to depart.

senses.d: To consider; to regard; to esteem; to account; to think; to judge.
q: I hold him but a fool.
I shall never hold that man my friend.
The Lord will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain.

senses.d: To bear, carry, or manage; as he holds himself erect; he holds his head high.
q: Let him hold his fingers thus.

Hold.etym: [OE. haldan, D. houden, OHG. hoten, Icel. halda, Dan. holde, Sw. hålla, Goth. haldan to feed, tend (the cattle); of unknown origin. Gf. Avast, Halt, Hod.]

senses.d: In general, to keep one's self in a given position or condition; to remain fixed. Hence:
Not to move; to halt; to stop; — mostly in the imperative.
q: And damned be him that first cries, “Hold, enough!”

senses.d: Not to give way; not to part or become separated; to remain unbroken or unsubdued.
q: Our force by land hath nobly held.

senses.d: Not to fail or be found wanting; to continue; to last; to endure a test or trial; to abide; to persist.
q: While our obedience holds.
The rule holds in land as all other commodities.

senses.d: Not to fall away, desert, or prove recreant; to remain attached; to cleave; — often with with, to, or for.
q: He will hold to the one and despise the other.

senses.d: To restrain one's self; to refrain.
q: His dauntless heart would fain have held From weeping, but his eyes rebelled.

senses.d: To derive right or title; — generally with of.
q: My crown is absolute, and holds of none.
His imagination holds immediately from nature.

senses.d: The act of holding, as in or with the hands or arms; the manner of holding, whether firm or loose; seizure; grasp; clasp; gripe; possession; — often used with the verbs take and lay.
q: Ne have I not twelve pence within mine hold.
Thou should'st lay hold upon him.
My soul took hold on thee.
Take fast hold of instruction.

senses.d: The authority or ground to take or keep; claim.
q: The law hath yet another hold on you.

senses.d: Binding power and influence.
q: Fear . . . by which God and his laws take the surest hold of.

senses.d: Something that may be grasped; means of support.
q: If a man be upon an high place without rails or good hold, he is ready to fall.

senses.d: A place of confinement; a prison; confinement; custody; guard.
q: They . . . put them in hold unto the next day.
King Richard, he is in the mighty hold Of Bolingbroke.

senses.d: A place of security; a fortified place; a fort; a castle; — often called a stronghold.
q: New comers in an ancient hold

senses.d: A character placed over or under a note or rest, and indicating that it is to be prolonged; — called also pause, and corona.
To stop in order to rob, often with the demand to hold up the hands.
The act or state of sustaining, grasping, or retaining.
A tenure; a farm or other estate held of another.
That which holds, binds, or influences.
The burden or chorus of a song.
Whole.
A hollow place or cavity; an excavation; a pit; an opening in or through a solid body, a fabric, etc.; a perforation; a rent; a fissure.
q: The holes where eyes should be.
The blind walls Were full of chinks and holes.
The priest took a chest, and bored a hole in the lid.

senses.d: An excavation in the ground, made by an animal to live in, or a natural cavity inhabited by an animal; hence, a low, narrow, or dark lodging or place; a mean habitation.
q: The foxes have holes, . . . but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head.

Hole.syn: Hollow; concavity; aperture; rent; fissure; crevice; orifice; interstice; perforation; excavation; pit; cave; den; cell.
Hole.etym: [OE. hol, hole, AS. hol, hole, cavern, from hol, a., hollow; akin to D. hol, OHG. hol, G. hohl, Dan. huul hollow, hul hole, Sw. hål, Icel. hola; prob. from the root of AS. helan to conceal. See Hele, Hell, and cf. Hold of a ship.]

senses.d: To cut, dig, or bore a hole or holes in; as, to hole a post for the insertion of rails or bars.
To drive into a hole, as an animal, or a billiard ball.
To go or get into a hole.
A small cavity used in some games, usually one into which a marble or ball is to be played or driven; hence, a score made by playing a marble or ball into such a hole, as in golf.
At Eton College, England, that part of the floor of the court between the step and the pepperbox.
Piously; with sanctity; in a holy manner.
Sacredly; inviolably.
The state or quality of being holy; perfect moral integrity or purity; freedom from sin; sanctity; innocence.
q: Who is like thee, glorious in holiness!

senses.d: The state of being hallowed, or consecrated to God or to his worship; sacredness.
q: Israel was holiness unto the Lord.

Holiness.syn: Piety; devotion; godliness; sanctity; sacredness; righteousness.

senses.d: Having an empty space or cavity, natural or artificial, within a solid substance; not solid; excavated in the interior; as, a hollow tree; a hollow sphere.
q: Hollow with boards shalt thou make it.

senses.d: Depressed; concave; gaunt; sunken.
q: With hollow eye and wrinkled brow.

senses.d: Reverberated from a cavity, or resembling such a sound; deep; muffled; as, a hollow roar.
Not sincere or faithful; false; deceitful; not sound; as, a hollow heart; a hollow friend.

Hollow.syn: Concave; sunken; low; vacant; empty; void; false; faithless; deceitful; treacherous.
Hollow.etym: [OE. holow, holgh, holf, AS. holh a hollow, hole. Cf. Hole.]

senses.d: A cavity, natural or artificial; an unfilled space within anything; a hole, a cavern; an excavation; as the hollow of the hand or of a tree.
A low spot surrounded by elevations; a depressed part of a surface; a concavity; a channel.
q: Forests grew Upon the barren hollows.
I hate the dreadful hollow behind the little wood.

senses.d: To make hollow, as by digging, cutting, or engraving; to excavate.
Wholly; completely; utterly; — chiefly after the verb to beat, and often with all; as, this story beats the other all hollow. See All, adv.
q: The more civilized so-called Caucasian races have beaten the Turks hollow in the struggle for existence.

senses.d: Hollo.
To shout; to hollo.
q: Whisperings and hollowings are alike to a deaf ear.

senses.d: To urge or call by shouting.
q: He has hollowed the hounds.

senses.d: Set apart to the service or worship of God; hallowed; sacred; reserved from profane or common use; holy vessels; a holy priesthood.
Spiritually whole or sound; of unimpaired innocence and virtue; free from sinful affections; pure in heart; godly; pious; irreproachable; guiltless; acceptable to God.
q: Now through her round of holy thought The Church our annual steps has brought.

Holy.etym: [OE. holi, hali, AS. hālig, fr. hæl health, salvation, happiness, fr. hāl whole, well; akin to OS. h�lag, D. & G. heilig, OHG. heilac, Dan. hellig, Sw. helig, Icel. heilagr. See Whole, and cf. Halibut, Halidom, Hallow, Hollyhock.]

senses.d: A religious festival.
A secular festival; a holiday.
One's own dwelling place; the house in which one lives; esp., the house in which one lives with his family; the habitual abode of one's family; also, one's birthplace.
q: The disciples went away again to their own home.
Home is the sacred refuge of our life.
Home! home! sweet, sweet home! There's no place like home.

senses.d: One's native land; the place or country in which one dwells; the place where one's ancestors dwell or dwelt.
The abiding place of the affections, especially of the domestic affections.
q: He entered in his house — his home no more, For without hearts there is no home.

senses.d: The locality where a thing is usually found, or was first found, or where it is naturally abundant; habitat; seat; as, the home of the pine.
q: Her eyes are homes of silent prayer.
Flandria, by plenty made the home of war.

senses.d: A place of refuge and rest; an asylum; as, a home for outcasts; a home for the blind; hence, esp., the grave; the final rest; also, the native and eternal dwelling place of the soul.
q: Man goeth to his long home, and the mourners go about the streets.

senses.d: The home base; he started for home.

Home.etym: [OE. hom, ham, AS. hām; akin to OS. hēm, D. & G. heim, Sw. hem, Dan. hiem, Icel. heimr abode, world, heima home, Goth. haims village, Lith. këmas, and perh. to Gr. κώμη village, or to E. hind a peasant; cf. Skr.kshēma abode, place of rest, security, kshi to dwell. √20, 220.]

senses.d: Of or pertaining to one's dwelling or country; domestic; not foreign; as home manufactures; home comforts.
Close; personal; pointed; as, a home thrust.
To one's home or country; as in the phrases, go home, come home, carry home.
Close; closely.
q: How home the charge reaches us, has been made out.
They come home to men's business and bosoms.

senses.d: To the place where it belongs; to the end of a course; to the full length; as, to drive a nail home; to ram a cartridge home.
q: Wear thy good rapier bare and put it home.

senses.d: In various games, the ultimate point aimed at in a progress; goal
The plate at which the batter stands.
The place of a player in front of an opponent's goal; also, the player.
Native; indigenous; not foreign.
Of or pertaining to the home or family.
q: Fireside enjoyments, homeborn happiness.

senses.d: A carrier pigeon remarkable for its ability to return home from a distance.

A Hebrew measure containing, as a liquid measure, ten baths, equivalent to fifty-five gallons, two quarts, one pint; and, as a dry measure, ten ephahs, equivalent to six bushels, two pecks, four quarts.
To pine; to lament; to long.
A kind of swelling in the cheek.
A stone of a fine grit, or a slab, as of metal, covered with an abrading substance or powder, used for sharpening cutting instruments, and especially for setting razors; an oilstone.

Hone.etym: [AS. hān; akin to Icel. hein, OSw. hen; cf. Skr. çāṇa, also çō, çi, to sharpen, and E. cone. √38, 228.]

senses.d: To sharpen on, or with, a hone; to rub on a hone in order to sharpen; as, to hone a razor.
To grumble; pine; lament; long.
Decent; honorable; suitable; becoming.
q: Belong what honest clothes you send forth to bleaching!

senses.d: Characterized by integrity or fairness and straight�forwardness in conduct, thought, speech, etc.; upright; just; equitable; trustworthy; truthful; sincere; free from fraud, guile, or duplicity; not false; — said of persons and acts, and of things to which a moral quality is imputed; as, an honest judge or merchant; an honest statement; an honest bargain; an honest business; an honest book; an honest confession.
q: An honest man's the noblest work of God.
An honest physician leaves his patient when he can contribute no farther to his health.
Look ye out among you seven men of honest report.
Provide things honest in the sight of all men.

senses.d: Open; frank; as, an honest countenance.
Chaste; faithful; virtuous.
q: Wives may be merry, and yet honest too.

Honest.syn: Upright; ingenuous; honorable; trusty; faithful; equitable; fair; just; rightful; sincere; frank; candid; genuine.
Honest.etym: [OE. honest, onest, OF. honeste, oneste, F. honnête, L. honestus, fr. honos, honor, honor. See Honor.]

senses.d: To adorn; to grace; to honor; to make becoming, appropriate, or honorable.

Honest.etym: [L. honestare to clothe or adorn with honor: cf. F. honester. See Honest, a.]

senses.d: Honorably; becomingly; decently.
In an honest manner; as, a contract honestly made; to live honestly; to speak honestly.
Honor; honorableness; dignity; propriety; suitableness; decency.
q: She derives her honesty and achieves her goodness.

senses.d: The quality or state of being honest; probity; fairness and straightforwardness of conduct, speech, etc.; integrity; sincerity; truthfulness; freedom from fraud or guile.
q: That we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty.

senses.d: Chastity; modesty.
q: To lay . . . siege to the honesty of this Ford's wife.

senses.d: Satin flower; the name of two cruciferous herbs having large flat pods, the round shining partitions of which are more beautiful than the blossom; — called also lunary and moonwort. Lunaria biennis is common honesty; L. rediva is perennial honesty.

Honesty.syn: Integrity; probity; uprightness; trustiness; faithfulness; honor; justice; equity; fairness; candor; plain-dealing; veracity; sincerity.
Honesty.etym: [OE. honeste, oneste, honor, OF. honesté, onesté (cf. F. honnêteté), L. honestas. See Honest, a.]

senses.d: A sweet viscid fluid, esp. that collected by bees from flowers of plants, and deposited in the cells of the honeycomb.
That which is sweet or pleasant, like honey.
q: The honey of his language.

senses.d: Sweet one; — a term of endearment.
q: Honey, you shall be well desired in Cyprus.

Honey.etym: [OE. honi, huni, AS. hunig; akin to OS. honeg, D. & G. honig, OHG. honag, honang, Icel. hunang, Sw. håning, Dan. honning, cf. Gr. � dust, Skr. kaa grain.]

senses.d: To be gentle, agreeable, or coaxing; to talk fondly; to use endearments; also, to be or become obsequiously courteous or complimentary; to fawn.
q: Rough to common men, But honey at the whisper of a lord.

senses.d: To make agreeable; to cover or sweeten with, or as with, honey.
q: Canst thou not honey me with fluent speech?

senses.d: A mass of hexagonal waxen cells, formed by bees, and used by them to hold their honey and their eggs.
Any substance, as a easting of iron, a piece of worm-eaten wood, or of triple, etc., perforated with cells like a honeycomb.
State; condition.
q: How could thou ween, through that disguised hood To hide thy state from being understood?

senses.d: A covering or garment for the head or the head and shoulders, often attached to the body garment
Anything resembling a hood in form or use
The endmost plank of a strake which reaches the stem or stern.

Hood.etym: [OE. hood, hod, AS. hōd; akin to D. hoed hat, G. hut, OHG. huot, also to E. hat, and prob. to E. heed. √13.]

senses.d: To cover with a hood; to furnish with a hood or hood-shaped appendage.
q: The friar hooded, and the monarch crowned.

senses.d: To cover; to hide; to blind.
q: While grace is saying, I'll hood mine eyes Thus with my hat, and sigh and say, “Amen.”

senses.d: The horny substance or case that covers or terminates the feet of certain animals, as horses, oxen, etc.
q: On burnished hooves his war horse trode.

senses.d: A hoofed animal; a beast.
q: Our cattle also shall go with us; there shall not a hoof be left behind.

Hoof.etym: [OE. hof, AS. hōf; akin to D. hoef, G. huf, OHG. huof, Icel. hōfr, Sw. hof, Dan. hov; cf. Russ. kopuito, Skr. çapha. √225.]

senses.d: To walk as cattle.
To be on a tramp; to foot.

A piece of metal, or other hard material, formed or bent into a curve or at an angle, for catching, holding, or sustaining anything; as, a hook for catching fish; a hook for fastening a gate; a boat hook, etc.
That part of a hinge which is fixed to a post, and on which a door or gate hangs and turns.
An implement for cutting grass or grain; a sickle; an instrument for cutting or lopping; a billhook.
q: Like slashing Bentley with his desperate hook.

senses.d: A snare; a trap.
A field sown two years in succession.
The projecting points of the thigh bones of cattle; — called also hook bones.

Hook.etym: [OE. hok, AS. hōc; cf. D. haak, G. hake, haken, OHG. hāko, hāgo, hāggo, Icel. haki, Sw. hake, Dan. hage. Cf. Arquebuse, Hagbut, Hake, Hatch a half door, Heckle.]

senses.d: To catch or fasten with a hook or hooks; to seize, capture, or hold, as with a hook, esp. with a disguised or baited hook; hence, to secure by allurement or artifice; to entrap; to catch; as, to hook a dress; to hook a trout.
q: Hook him, my poor dear, . . . at any sacrifice.

senses.d: To seize or pierce with the points of the horns, as cattle in attacking enemies; to gore.
To steal.
To bend; to curve as a hook.
A spit or narrow cape of sand or gravel turned landward at the outer end; as, Sandy Hook.
To move or go with a sudden turn;
to make off; to clear out; — often with it.
To move by successive leaps, as toads do; to spring or jump on one foot; to skip, as birds do.
q: hopping from spray to spray.

senses.d: To walk lame; to limp; to halt.
To dance.

Hop.etym: [OE. hoppen to hop, leap, dance, AS. hoppian; akin to Icel. & Sw. hoppa, Dan. hoppe, D. huppelen, G. hüpfen.]

senses.d: A leap on one leg, as of a boy; a leap, as of a toad; a jump; a spring.
A dance; esp., an informal dance of ball.
A climbing plant (Humulus Lupulus), having a long, twining, annual stalk. It is cultivated for its fruit (hops).
The catkin or strobilaceous fruit of the hop, much used in brewing to give a bitter taste.
The fruit of the dog-rose. See Hip.

Hop.etym: [OE. hoppe; akin to D. hop, hoppe, OHG. hopfo, G. hopfen; cf. LL. hupa, W. hopez, Armor. houpez, and Icel. humall, SW. & Dan. humle.]

senses.d: To impregnate with hops.
To gather hops. [Perhaps only in the form Hopping, vb. n.]
A sloping plain between mountain ridges.
A small bay; an inlet; a haven.

Hope.etym: [Cf. Icel. hōp a small bay or inlet.]

senses.d: A desire of some good, accompanied with an expectation of obtaining it, or a belief that it is obtainable; an expectation of something which is thought to be desirable; confidence; pleasing expectancy.
q: The hypocrite's hope shall perish.
He wished, but not with hope.
New thoughts of God, new hopes of Heaven.

senses.d: One who, or that which, gives hope, furnishes ground of expectation, or promises desired good.
q: The Lord will be the hope of his people.
A young gentleman of great hopes, whose love of learning was highly commendable.

senses.d: That which is hoped for; an object of hope.
q: Lavina is thine elder brother's hope.

Hope.etym: [AS., akin to D. hoop, hope, Sw. hopp, Dan. haab, MHG. hoffe. Hope in forlorn hope is different word. See Forlorn hope, under Forlorn.]

senses.d: To entertain or indulge hope; to cherish a desire of good, or of something welcome, with expectation of obtaining it or belief that it is obtainable; to expect; — usually followed by for.
q: But I will hope continually.

senses.d: To place confidence; to trust with confident expectation of good; — usually followed by in.
q: Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted within me? Hope thou in God.

Hope.etym: [AS. hopian; akin to D. hopen, Sw. hopp�, Dan. haabe, G. hoffen. See 2nd Hope.]

senses.d: To desire with expectation or with belief in the possibility or prospect of obtaining; to look forward to as a thing desirable, with the expectation of obtaining it; to cherish hopes of.
q: We hope no other from your majesty.
hopeth all things.

senses.d: To expect; to fear.

A hard, projecting, and usually pointed organ, growing upon the heads of certain animals, esp. of the ruminants, as cattle, goats, and the like. The hollow horns of the Ox family consist externally of true horn, and are never shed.
The antler of a deer, which is of bone throughout, and annually shed and renewed.

Any natural projection or excrescence from an animal, resembling or thought to resemble a horn in substance or form; esp.: (a) A projection from the beak of a bird, as in the hornbill. (b) A tuft of feathers on the head of a bird, as in the horned owl. (c) A hornlike projection from the head or thorax of an insect, or the head of a reptile, or fish. (d) A sharp spine in front of the fins of a fish, as in the horned pout.
An incurved, tapering and pointed appendage found in the flowers of the milkweed (Asclepias).
Something made of a horn, or in resemblance of a horn
One of the curved ends of a crescent; esp., an extremity or cusp of the moon when crescent-shaped.
q: The moon Wears a wan circle round her blunted horns.

senses.d: The curving extremity of the wing of an army or of a squadron drawn up in a crescentlike form.
q: Sharpening in mooned horns Their phalanx.

senses.d: The tough, fibrous material of which true horns are composed, being, in the Ox family, chiefly albuminous, with some phosphate of lime; also, any similar substance, as that which forms the hoof crust of horses, sheep, and cattle; as, a spoon of horn.
A symbol of strength, power, glory, exaltation, or pride.
q: The Lord is . . . the horn of my salvation.

senses.d: An emblem of a cuckold; — used chiefly in the plural.

Horn.etym: [AS. horn; akin to D. horen, hoorn, G., Icel., Sw., & Dan. horn, Goth. haúrn, W., Gael., & Ir. corn, L. cornu, Gr. �, and perh. also to E. cheer, cranium, cerebral; cf. Skr. çiras head. Cf. Carat, Corn on the foot, Cornea, Corner, Cornet, Cornucopia, Hart.]

senses.d: To furnish with horns; to give the shape of a horn to.
To cause to wear horns; to cuckold.

A large, strong wasp. The European species (Vespa crabro) is of a dark brown and yellow color. It is very pugnacious, and its sting is very severe. Its nest is constructed of a paperlike material, and the layers of comb are hung together by columns. The American white-faced hornet (V. maculata) is larger and has similar habits.

Hornet.etym: [AS. hyrnet; akin to OHG. hornaz, hornuz, G. horniss; perh. akin to E. horn, and named from the sound it makes as if blowing the horn; but more prob. akin to D. horzel, Lith. szirszone, L. crabo.]

senses.d: Exciting, or tending to excite, horror or fear; dreadful; terrible; shocking; hideous; as, a horrible sight; a horrible story; a horrible murder.
q: A dungeon horrible on all sides round.

Horrible.syn: Dreadful; frightful; fearful; terrible; awful; terrific; shocking; hideous; horrid.
Horrible.etym: [OE. horrible, orrible, OF. horrible, orrible, F. horrible, fr. L. horribilis, fr. horrere. See Horror.]

senses.d: In a manner to excite horror; dreadfully; terribly.
A bristling up; a rising into roughness; tumultuous movement.
q: Such fresh horror as you see driven through the wrinkled waves.

senses.d: A shaking, shivering, or shuddering, as in the cold fit which precedes a fever; in old medical writings, a chill of less severity than a rigor, and more marked than an algor.
A painful emotion of fear, dread, and abhorrence; a shuddering with terror and detestation; the feeling inspired by something frightful and shocking.
q: How could this, in the sight of heaven, without horrors of conscience be uttered?

senses.d: That which excites horror or dread, or is horrible; gloom; dreariness.
q: Breathes a browner horror on the woods.

senses.d: A hoofed quadruped of the genus Equus; especially, the domestic horse (E. caballus), which was domesticated in Egypt and Asia at a very early period. It has six broad molars, on each side of each jaw, with six incisors, and two canine teeth, both above and below. The mares usually have the canine teeth rudimentary or wanting. The horse differs from the true asses, in having a long, flowing mane, and the tail bushy to the base. Unlike the asses it has callosities, or chestnuts, on all its legs. The horse excels in strength, speed, docility, courage, and nobleness of character, and is used for drawing, carrying, bearing a rider, and like purposes.
The male of the genus horse, in distinction from the female or male; usually, a castrated male.
Mounted soldiery; cavalry; — used without the plural termination; as, a regiment of horse; — distinguished from foot.
q: The armies were appointed, consisting of twenty-five thousand horse and foot.

senses.d: A frame with legs, used to support something; as, a clotheshorse, a sawhorse, etc.
A frame of timber, shaped like a horse, on which soldiers were made to ride for punishment.
Anything, actual or figurative, on which one rides as on a horse; a hobby.

A mass of earthy matter, or rock of the same character as the wall rock, occurring in the course of a vein, as of coal or ore; hence, to take horse — said of a vein — is to divide into branches for a distance.
A breastband for a leadsman.

Horse.etym: [AS. hors; akin to OS. hros, D. & OHG. ros, G. ross, Icel. hross; and perh. to L. currere to run, E. course, current Cf. Walrus.]

senses.d: To provide with a horse, or with horses; to mount on, or as on, a horse.
To sit astride of; to bestride.
To cover, as a mare; — said of the male.
To take or carry on the back; as, the keeper, horsing a deer.
To place on the back of another, or on a wooden horse, etc., to be flogged; to subject to such punishment.
To get on horseback.
A translation or other illegitimate aid in study or examination; — called also trot, pony, Dobbin.
Horseplay; tomfoolery.
The back of a horse.
An extended ridge of sand, gravel, and bowlders, in a half-stratified condition.
A rider on horseback; one skilled in the management of horses; a mounted man.
A mounted soldier; a cavalryman.
A land crab of the genus Ocypoda, living on the coast of Brazil and the West Indies, noted for running very swiftly.
A Hebrew exclamation of praise to the Lord, or an invocation of blessings.
q: Hosanna to the Son of David.

Hosanna.etym: [Gr. �, fr. Heb. hōshī'āh nnāsave now, save, we pray, hōshīa' to save (Hiphil, a causative form, of yāsha') + nā, a particle.]

senses.d: The act or practice of one who is hospitable; reception and entertainment of strangers or guests without reward, or with kind and generous liberality.
q: Given to hospitality.
And little recks to find the way to heaven By doing deeds of hospitality.

senses.d: The consecrated wafer, believed to be the body of Christ, which in the Mass is offered as a sacrifice; also, the bread before consecration.

Host.etym: [LL. hostia sacrifice, victim, from hostire to strike.]

senses.d: An army; a number of men gathered for war.
q: A host so great as covered all the field.

senses.d: Any great number or multitude; a throng.
q: And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host praising God.
All at once I saw a crowd, A host, of golden daffodils.

Host.etym: [OE. host, ost, OF. host, ost, fr. L. hostis enemy, LL., army. See Guest, and cf. Host a landlord.]

senses.d: One who receives or entertains another, whether gratuitously or for compensation; one from whom another receives food, lodging, or entertainment; a landlord.
q: Time is like a fashionable host, That slightly shakes his parting guest by the hand.

Host.etym: [OE. host, ost, OF. hoste, oste, F. hôte, from L. hospes a stranger who is treated as a guest, he who treats another as his guest, a hostl prob. fr. hostis stranger, enemy (akin to E. guest a visitor) + potis able; akin to Skr. pati master, lord. See Host an army, Possible, and cf. Hospitable, Hotel

senses.d: To give entertainment to.
To lodge at an inn; to take up entertainment.
Any animal or plant affording lodgment or subsistence to a parasitic or commensal organism. Thus a tree is a host of an air plant growing upon it.
A person given as a pledge or security for the performance of the conditions of a treaty or stipulations of any kind, on the performance of which the person is to be released.
q: Your hostages I have, so have you mine; And we shall talk before we fight.
He that hath a wife and children hath given hostages to fortune.

Hostage.etym: [OE. hostage, OF. hostage, ostage, F. ôtage, LL. hostaticus, ostaticum, for hospitaticum, fr. L. hospes guest, host. The first meaning is, the state of a guest, hospitality; hence, the state of a hostage (treated as a guest); and both these meanings occur in Old French. See Host a landlord.]

senses.d: Having much sensible heat; exciting the feeling of warmth in a great degree; very warm; — opposed to cold, and exceeding warm in degree; as, a hot stove; hot water or air.
Characterized by heat, ardor, or animation; easily excited; firely; vehement; passionate; violent; eager.
q: Achilles is impatient, hot, and revengeful.
There was mouthing in hot haste.

senses.d: Lustful; lewd; lecherous.
Acrid; biting; pungent; as, hot as mustard.

Hot.syn: Burning; fiery; fervid; glowing; eager; animated; brisk; vehement; precipitate; violent; furious; ardent; fervent; impetuous; irascible; passionate; hasty; excitable.
Hot.etym: [OE. hot, hat, AS. hāt; akin to OS. hēt, D. heet, OHG. heiz, G. heiss, Icel. heitr, Sw. het, Dan. heed, hed; cf. Goth. heitō fever, hais torch. Cf. Heat.]

senses.d: In a hot or fiery manner; ardently; vehemently; violently; hastily; as, a hotly pursued.
In a lustful manner; lustfully.
Same as Hock, a joint.
Same as Hock, to hamstring.
An adz; a hoe.
To cut with a hoe.
The twenty-fourth part of a day; sixty minutes.
The time of the day, as expressed in hours and minutes, and indicated by a timepiece; as, what is the hour? At what hour shall we meet?
Fixed or appointed time; conjuncture; a particular time or occasion; as, the hour of greatest peril; the man for the hour.
q: Woman, . . . mine hour is not yet come.
This is your hour, and the power of darkness.

senses.d: Certain prayers to be repeated at stated times of the day, as matins and vespers.
A measure of distance traveled.
q: Vilvoorden, three hours from Brussels.

Hour.etym: [OE. hour, our, hore, ure, OF. hore, ore, ure, F. heure, L. hora, fr. Gr. �, orig., a definite space of time, fixed by natural laws; hence, a season, the time of the day, an hour. See Year, and cf. Horologe, Horoscope.]

senses.d: Goddess of the seasons, or of the hours of the day.
q: Lo! where the rosy-blosomed Hours, Fair Venus' train, appear.

Hours.etym: [A translation of L. Horae (Gr. �). See Hour.]

senses.d: A structure intended or used as a habitation or shelter for animals of any kind; but especially, a building or edifice for the habitation of man; a dwelling place, a mansion.
q: Houses are built to live in; not to look on.
Bees with smoke and doves with noisome stench Are from their hives and houses driven away.

senses.d: Household affairs; domestic concerns; particularly in the phrase to keep house. See below.
Those who dwell in the same house; a household.
q: One that feared God with all his house.

senses.d: A family of ancestors, descendants, and kindred; a race of persons from the same stock; a tribe; especially, a noble family or an illustrious race; as, the house of Austria; the house of Hanover; the house of Israel.
q: The last remaining pillar of their house, The one transmitter of their ancient name.

senses.d: One of the estates of a kingdom or other government assembled in parliament or legislature; a body of men united in a legislative capacity; as, the House of Lords; the House of Commons; the House of Representatives; also, a quorum of such a body. See Congress, and Parliament.
A firm, or commercial establishment.
A public house; an inn; a hotel.

A twelfth part of the heavens, as divided by six circles intersecting at the north and south points of the horizon, used by astrologers in noting the positions of the heavenly bodies, and casting horoscopes or nativities. The houses were regarded as fixed in respect to the horizon, and numbered from the one at the eastern horizon, called the ascendant, first house, or house of life, downward, or in the direction of the earth's revolution, the stars and planets passing through them in the reverse order every twenty-four hours.
A square on a chessboard, regarded as the proper place of a piece.
An audience; an assembly of hearers, as at a lecture, a theater, etc.; as, a thin or a full house.
The body, as the habitation of the soul.
q: This mortal house I'll ruin, Do Cæsar what he can.

senses.d: The grave.

House.etym: [OE. hous, hus, AS. h�s; akin to OS. & OFries. h�s, D. huis, OHG. h�s, G. haus, Icel. h�s, Sw. hus, Dan. huus, Goth. gudh�s, house of God, temple; and prob. to E. hide to conceal. See Hide, and cf. Hoard, Husband, Hussy, Husting.]

senses.d: To take or put into a house; to shelter under a roof; to cover from the inclemencies of the weather; to protect by covering; as, to house one's family in a comfortable home; to house farming utensils; to house cattle.
q: At length have housed me in a humble shed.
House your choicest carnations, or rather set them under a penthouse.

senses.d: To drive to a shelter.
To admit to residence; to harbor.
q: Palladius wished him to house all the Helots.

senses.d: To deposit and cover, as in the grave.
To stow in a safe place; to take down and make safe; as, to house the upper spars.
To take shelter or lodging; to abide to dwell; to lodge.
q: You shall not house with me.

senses.d: To have a position in one of the houses. See House, n., 8.
Those who dwell under the same roof and compose a family.
q: And calls, without affecting airs, His household twice a day to prayers.

senses.d: A line of ancestory; a race or house.
Belonging to the house and family; domestic; as, household furniture; household affairs.
The master or head of a family; one who occupies a house with his family.
q: Towns in which almost every householder was an English Protestant.

senses.d: In what manner or way; by what means or process.
q: How can a man be born when he is old?

senses.d: To what degree or extent, number or amount; in what proportion; by what measure or quality.
q: O, how love I thy law! it is my meditation all the day.
By how much they would diminish the present extent of the sea, so much they would impair the fertility, and fountains, and rivers of the earth.

senses.d: For what reason; from what cause.
q: How now, my love! why is your cheek so pale?

senses.d: In what state, condition, or plight.
q: How, and with what reproach, shall I return?

senses.d: By what name, designation, or title.
q: How art thou called?

senses.d: At what price; how dear.
q: How a score of ewes now?
Let me beg you — don't say “How?” for “What?”

How.etym: [OE. how, hou, hu, hwu, AS. h�, from the same root as hwā, hwæt, who, what, pron. interrog.; akin to OS. hwōw, D. hoe, cf. G. wie how, Goth. hwē wherewith, hwaiwa how. √182. See Who, and cf. Why.]

senses.d: Be it as it may; nevertheless; notwithstanding; although; albeit; yet; but; however.
q: The Moor — howbeit that I endure him not - Is of a constant, loving, noble nature.

senses.d: To utter a loud, protracted, mournful sound or cry, as dogs and wolves often do.
q: And dogs in corners set them down to howl.
Methought a legion of foul fiends Environ'd me about, and howled in my ears.

senses.d: To utter a sound expressive of distress; to cry aloud and mournfully; to lament; to wail.
q: Howl ye, for the day of the Lord is at hand.

senses.d: To make a noise resembling the cry of a wild beast.
q: Wild howled the wind.

Howl.etym: [OE. houlen, hulen; akin to D. huilen, MHG. hiulen, hiuweln, OHG. hiuwilōn to exult, h�wo owl, Dan. hyle to howl.]

senses.d: To utter with outcry.
The protracted, mournful cry of a dog or a wolf, or other like sound.
A prolonged cry of distress or anguish; a wail.
In what manner soever; to whatever degree or extent; however.
q: I am glad he's come, howsoever he comes.

senses.d: Although; though; however.
Very large; enormous; immense; excessive; — used esp. of material bulk, but often of qualities, extent, etc.; as, a huge ox; a huge space; a huge difference.
q: Doth it not flow as hugely as the sea.

Huge.syn: Enormous; gigantic; colossal; immense; prodigious; vast.

senses.d: Near the ground; not high or lofty; not pretentious or magnificent; unpretending; unassuming; as, a humble cottage.
q: Thy humble nest built on the ground.

senses.d: Thinking lowly of one's self; claiming little for one's self; not proud, arrogant, or assuming; thinking one's self ill-deserving or unworthy, when judged by the demands of God; lowly; weak; modest.
q: God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble.
She should be humble who would please.
Without a humble imitation of the divine Author of our . . . religion we can never hope to be a happy nation.

Humble.etym: [F., fr. L. humilis on the ground, low, fr. humus the earth, ground. See Homage, and cf. Chameleon, Humiliate.]

senses.d: Hornless. See Hummel.
To bring low; to reduce the power, independence, or exaltation of; to lower; to abase; to humilate.
q: Here, take this purse, thou whom the heaven's plagues Have humbled to all strokes.
The genius which humbled six marshals of France.

senses.d: To make humble or lowly in mind; to abase the pride or arrogance of; to reduce the self-sufficiently of; to make meek and submissive; — often used rexlexively.
q: Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you.

Humble.syn: To abase; lower; depress; humiliate; mortify; disgrace; degrade.

senses.d: The quality of being humble; humility; meekness.
With humility; lowly.
The act of humiliating or humbling; abasement of pride; mortification.
The state of being humiliated, humbled, or reduced to lowliness or submission.
q: The former was a humiliation of Deity; the latter a humiliation of manhood.

senses.d: The state or quality of being humble; freedom from pride and arrogance; lowliness of mind; a modest estimate of one's own worth; a sense of one's own unworthiness through imperfection and sinfulness; self-abasement; humbleness.
q: Serving the Lord with all humility of mind.

senses.d: An act of submission or courtesy.
q: With these humilities they satisfied the young king.

Humility.etym: [OE. humilite, OF. humilité, humelité, F. humilité, fr. L. humiliatis. See Humble.]

senses.d: The product of ten multiplied by ten, or the number of ten times ten; a collection or sum, consisting of ten times ten units or objects; five score. Also, a symbol representing one hundred units, as 100 or C.
q: With many hundreds treading on his heels.

senses.d: A division of a country in England, supposed to have originally contained a hundred families, or freemen.

Hundred.etym: [OE. hundred, AS. hundred a territorial division; hund hundred + a word akin to Goth. ga-raþjan to count, L. ratio reckoning, account; akin to OS. hunderod, hund, D. hondred, G. hundert, OHG. also hunt, Icel. hundrað, Dan. hundrede, Sw. hundra, hundrade, Goth. hund, Lith. szimtas, Russ. sto, W. cant

senses.d: Ten times ten; five score; as, a hundred dollars.
A hundred times as much or as many.
q: He shall receive as hundredfold now in this time.

senses.d: Coming last of a hundred successive individuals or units.
Forming one of a hundred equal parts into which anything is divided; the tenth of a tenth.
One of a hundred equal parts into which one whole is, or may be, divided; the quotient of a unit divided by a hundred.

A hunter.

senses.d: A member of an ancient people (or perhaps group of peoples) whose settlements extended from Armenia westward into Asia Minor and southward into Palestine. They are known to have been met along the Orontes as early as 1500 b. c., and were often at war with the Egyptians and Assyrians. Especially in the north they developed a considerable civilization, of which numerous monuments and inscriptions are extant. Authorities are not agreed as to their race. While several attempts have been made to decipher the Hittite characters, little progress has yet been made.
